decisionNodes.stem: Which study design matches how the investigators selected participants, handled the study intervention and measured the clinical outcome described in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Cross-sectional study
answerChoices.rationale: Current device use and reflux symptoms are recorded together, without outcome-based recruitment or follow-up. Those features define this cross-sectional snapshot.

answerChoices.label: Case-control study
answerChoices.rationale: Case-control recruitment would depend on outcome status. The exhibit explicitly says recruitment does not depend on the current symptom findings.

answerChoices.label: Prospective cohort study
answerChoices.rationale: A prospective cohort would organize exposure groups and observe later outcomes. This survey has no follow-up after the same-visit measurements.

answerChoices.label: Randomized experiment
answerChoices.rationale: A randomized experiment requires investigator assignment. This survey records device use and symptoms without assigning a device or study arm.

decisionNodes.explanation: This is a cross-sectional survey: device use and current reflux symptoms were recorded together, without outcome-based recruitment, subsequent follow-up or investigator-assigned intervention.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A cross-sectional study records exposure and outcome at one time, giving a snapshot. Here device use and current symptoms are measured together, without outcome-based recruitment, assignment or follow-up. Remember what the study actually observed. A report title cannot create a time sequence or treatment allocation that the design never supplied.

decisionNodes.stem: Which problem most directly threatens the unadjusted intervention-outcome comparison when study site relates to both?

answerChoices.label: Confounding by study site
answerChoices.rationale: Site relates to both intervention use and the outcome, and the comparison ignores it. Their mixed association is the stated confounding concern.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit describes an ignored third factor in the comparison, not differential entry into the sample. That is the confounding rather than selection mechanism supplied.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from recall
answerChoices.rationale: No unequal recall or outcome-recording method is described. The stated problem is the ignored relationship of site with both exposure and outcome.

answerChoices.label: Random error from sample size
answerChoices.rationale: More observations do not automatically remove the systematic mixing with site. Sample-size variation is not the primary mechanism described.

decisionNodes.explanation: Study site is a confounder in this exercise because it relates to both intervention use and the outcome and is ignored in the comparison.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Confounding occurs when an exposure comparison is mixed with another associated factor. Here site relates to both intervention use and the outcome, so the unadjusted association may combine those relationships. Remember the third-factor question: what else differs with exposure and outcome? More observations do not automatically remove that systematic problem.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational hernia reinforcement material study: Study site predicts both material use and two-year hernia recurrence. The unadjusted comparison ignores site; that relationship is stipulated for this exercise, not a clinical risk-factor claim. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

decisionNodes.stem: Which bias most directly limits the claim about all eligible surgical patients when recruitment covers daytime operations only?

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from daytime-only recruitment
answerChoices.rationale: Daytime encounters alone are used to make an all-patients claim. The missing nighttime surgical patients create the stated selection concern even with a large daytime sample.

answerChoices.label: Confounding by an unmeasured patient characteristic
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied mechanism is who entered the audit. No patient factor relating both exposure and outcome is identified as the primary concern.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from unequal recall windows
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit does not describe unequal recall. It describes exclusion of nighttime surgical patients from an all-patients conclusion.

answerChoices.label: Random error from insufficient sample precision
answerChoices.rationale: A large daytime sample can still exclude the target population of nighttime surgical patients. Greater sampling precision does not repair that selection problem.

decisionNodes.explanation: Daytime-only sampling creates the stated selection concern. Adding more daytime surgical patients does not supply the missing nighttime surgical observations needed for the all-patients conclusion.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Selection bias concerns which observations enter the study. A large daytime-only sample still leaves nighttime surgical patients outside an audit presented as applying to all eligible surgical patients. Sample size cannot repair that missing coverage. Distinguish this selection problem from confounding within the comparison or inconsistent measurement after people have entered it.

exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational thyroglossal-cyst dissection technique study: Investigators enroll daytime operations and no nighttime operations, yet present their thirty-day SSI conclusion as applying to all eligible surgical patients. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

decisionNodes.stem: Which information problem most directly threatens the outcome comparison when one group reports immediately and the other recalls events six months later?

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from unequal recall
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate recording in one group and recall six months later in the other use unequal measurement processes. That can systematically distort the recorded contrast.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: The difference concerns how outcomes were recorded after entry, rather than how people were selected for the study.

answerChoices.label: Confounding by baseline study site
answerChoices.rationale: No baseline site factor is supplied as relating exposure and the outcome. The stated concern is the unequal reporting schedule.

answerChoices.label: Random error from natural variation
answerChoices.rationale: The groups are measured by different recall processes. That systematic difference is not simply random variation that a larger sample necessarily removes.

decisionNodes.explanation: The primary concern is measurement bias from unequal recall schedules. The groups' recorded outcomes may differ because one reports immediately and the other recalls much later.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Measurement bias can arise when groups' outcomes are recorded differently. Immediate reports and recall six months later use unequal measurement processes, so a difference in reports may reflect how the outcomes were remembered. This is distinct from who was recruited or which baseline factor confounds the comparison. Larger samples do not equalize the reporting methods.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational calf-stimulation device study: One group reports postoperative DVT events immediately; the other recalls those events six months later. The reporting schedules differ; no real device effect is supplied. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
Testing and Diagnosis for Venous Thromboembolism

decisionNodes.stem: Which limitation remains after adjustment when an important factor related to both sensor choice and recorded outcomes was not measured?

answerChoices.label: Residual confounding by unmeasured factors
answerChoices.rationale: Unrecorded follow-up access differences relate to intervention choice and the outcome. Adjustment for other factors leaves that potential confounding unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Random error from the sampling process
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit identifies an unrecorded associated factor, not just sampling variability. Greater precision would not supply the missing follow-up access information.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: No enrollment mechanism is described as the primary concern. The known limitation is confounding by follow-up access differences absent from the model.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from inconsistent outcome recording
answerChoices.rationale: No inconsistent outcome-recording process is supplied. The gap is a relevant factor the model could not adjust for because it was not recorded.

decisionNodes.explanation: Residual confounding remains because relevant follow-up access differences were not measured. Adjusting for site and procedure category does not automatically account for that unrecorded factor.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Adjustment can address recorded factors without accounting for unrecorded ones. Follow-up access still relates to both intervention choice and the outcome, so residual confounding remains possible despite adjustment for site and procedure category. Remember that an adjusted label is not a guarantee of an unconfounded result; ask which relevant differences the model could actually use.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational anesthesia monitoring sensor study: The model adjusts for measured site and procedure category. Follow-up access relates to both sensor choice and recorded recognition of concerning intraoperative changes, but important access differences were not recorded. These relationships are stipulated, not general clinical risk-factor claims. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

decisionNodes.stem: What is the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's sensitivity in the separate constructed validation cohort shown in the exhibit?

answerChoices.rationale: Of the 100 people with the condition, 90 screen positive: 90/(90 + 10) = 90%. This is the condition-present denominator sensitivity requires.
Ten of 100 people with the condition screen negative. That is the false-negative fraction, not the positive fraction requested for sensitivity.
The calculation 90/(90 + 30) = 75% starts with all positive screens. That gives positive predictive value rather than sensitivity.
The calculation 70/(30 + 70) = 70% starts with people without the condition. It gives specificity, not sensitivity.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use the condition-present row: 90/(90 + 10) = 90% sensitivity. The positive-result column answers a different question, and this practice table is not a personal risk estimate.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Sensitivity starts with people who have the condition by the reference assessment: how many tested positive? Here 90 of 100 did, giving 90%. Remember: sensitivity begins with condition present, not with a positive or negative screen. These practice counts explain the measure; they do not calculate this patient's probability after a negative result.

answerChoices.rationale: Of the 100 people without the condition, 95 screen negative: 95/(5 + 95) = 95%. This is specificity.
Five of the 100 people without the condition screen positive. That gives the false-positive fraction, the opposite screen result from the one used for specificity.
The calculation 80/(80 + 20) = 80% uses the condition-present row and gives sensitivity. Specificity starts with condition absent.
The calculation 80/(80 + 5) is about 94%. It uses the positive-screen column to give positive predictive value, not specificity.

decisionNodes.explanation: Specificity is 95/(5 + 95) = 95%, using everyone without the condition as the denominator. It is not the proportion of positive results that are correct.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Specificity asks how often the screen is negative among people without the condition. In this table, 95 of 100 condition-absent people test negative, giving 95%. Start with condition absent. Starting with positive screens would instead ask about positive predictive value, which is a different measure and denominator.

decisionNodes.stem: How does the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's positive predictive value change between the hypothetical populations when sensitivity and specificity remain fixed as stated?

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value increases
answerChoices.rationale: With sensitivity and specificity fixed, the higher-prevalence population has a greater true-positive share among positive screens. This supports an increase, without an exact percentage.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value decreases
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction: higher prevalence increases the true-positive share among positives under the fixed-test assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value stays fixed
answerChoices.rationale: Fixed sensitivity and specificity do not fix positive predictive value. Prevalence also determines the mix of true and false positives.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value is indeterminate
answerChoices.rationale: An exact percentage would need more numbers, but the direction follows from higher prevalence with fixed test characteristics. That direction is not indeterminate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Positive predictive value increases under the stated fixed-test assumptions because prevalence is higher. The exhibit supports the direction of change without supplying an exact personal probability.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Positive predictive value asks what share of positive results come from people with the condition. With sensitivity and specificity held fixed, higher prevalence makes true positives a larger share of positives, so predictive value rises. Remember that the test and the tested population both matter; this comparison gives direction, not a personal percentage.

decisionNodes.stem: Among positive results in the separate constructed validation cohort, what is the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's positive predictive value?

answerChoices.rationale: Start with all positive screens: 40 + 10 = 50. Forty had the condition, so positive predictive value is 40/50 = 80%.
The calculation 30/(10 + 30) = 75% uses the condition-absent row. It answers a specificity question, not the positive-screen question asked.
The calculation 10/(40 + 10) = 20% is the false-positive share among positives. The requested predictive value counts true positives instead.
The calculation 40/(40 + 20) is about 67%. It begins with people who have the condition and therefore calculates sensitivity.

decisionNodes.explanation: Read the positive-screen column: 40 true positives and 10 false positives. Positive predictive value is 40/50 = 80% for these practice data.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Positive predictive value asks, of all positive results, how many were true positives? Its denominator includes true and false positives. Here 40 of 50 positives had the condition, giving 80%. Sensitivity instead starts with people known to have the condition. Remember which group the question starts with before choosing a row or column.

answerChoices.label: Different prevalence in the tested populations
answerChoices.rationale: Prevalence can change the true-positive share among positive results even with identical testing processes, sensitivity, and specificity. It is a possible explanation, not an exact value.

answerChoices.label: Different sensitivity in the tested populations
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit explicitly keeps sensitivity the same. A sensitivity difference cannot explain this exercise without contradicting that condition.

answerChoices.label: Different specificity in the tested populations
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit explicitly keeps specificity the same. This proposed explanation changes an assumption that was held fixed.

answerChoices.label: Different definitions of a positive test result
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit keeps the testing process and definition of positive the same. Reclassifying results contradicts that supplied comparison.

decisionNodes.explanation: Different prevalence can produce different positive predictive values despite identical test characteristics. The exhibit explicitly holds sensitivity, specificity, and result definitions constant.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Sensitivity and specificity describe results within condition-status groups; positive predictive value starts with positive results. Changing prevalence can change the mix of true and false positives even when those test characteristics stay fixed. Here prevalence is a possible explanation. The information does not supply its exact value or prove a personal diagnosis.

decisionNodes.stem: What risk ratio compares exposed with unexposed participants for the clinical outcome in the constructed cohort?

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: Divide exposed risk by unexposed risk: 0.20/0.10 = 2.0. The inputs are probabilities, so the result is a risk ratio.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: The quotient 0.20/0.10 compares risks, not odds. Calling that number an odds ratio changes the scale without doing an odds calculation.

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: The value 0.5 comes from 0.10/0.20, reversing the requested exposed-versus-unexposed direction.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: This both reverses the comparison and assigns an odds label to a calculation of probabilities. Neither change preserves the requested estimate.

decisionNodes.explanation: Dividing the exposed risk by the unexposed risk gives 0.20/0.10 = 2.0, a risk ratio. That calculation does not become an odds ratio by relabeling it.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Risk is a probability; a risk ratio divides one group's probability by the comparator's. Here 20%/10% = 2.0 for exposed versus unexposed over 30 days. An odds ratio compares odds instead. Remember both the scale and direction: reversing the groups gives a reciprocal, while changing the label changes the claimed measure.

decisionNodes.stem: For colon-cancer recurrence over two years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Subtracting gives 0.10; 1/0.10 = 10 for the specified outcome over two years.

answerChoices.label: ARR 50 percentage points; NNT 2 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The outcome risk halves relative to its 20% starting value, but falls by 10 percentage points, not 50. The relative wording does not supply this ARR or NNT.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 100 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The absolute difference is right, but its reciprocal uses the proportion 0.10: 1/0.10 = 10, not 100.

answerChoices.label: ARR 5 percentage points; NNT 20 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: An NNT of 20 would correspond to an absolute difference of 0.05. These practice risks differ by 0.10 instead.

decisionNodes.explanation: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Their difference is 0.10, giving ARR 10 percentage points and NNT 10 for the specified two-year outcome.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Calculate each group's risk first, then subtract intervention risk from comparator risk. Here 20% minus 10% is 10 percentage points, so NNT is 1/0.10 = 10 over two years. Half the starting risk and a 10-point absolute drop describe the same practice numbers; keep the outcome, comparator, and period attached.

decisionNodes.stem: For cutaneous-SCC recurrence over three years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 5 percentage points; NNT 20 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: First divide within each group: 30/200 = 0.15 and 10/100 = 0.10. ARR is 0.05 and its reciprocal is NNT 20 over three years.

answerChoices.label: ARR 20 percentage points; NNT 5 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: Subtracting 30 and 10 events ignores that the groups contain 200 and 100 people. Risks, rather than raw counts, must be subtracted.

answerChoices.label: ARR 33 percentage points; NNT 3 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: About 33% describes the relative reduction from 15% to 10%. The absolute drop is five percentage points, giving NNT 20.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: The comparator risk is 30/200 = 15%, not 20%. Using the actual denominator gives a five-point difference rather than ten.

decisionNodes.explanation: First calculate risks: 30/200 = 0.15 and 10/100 = 0.10. ARR is 0.05, or five percentage points, and three-year NNT is 20.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Unequal group sizes make raw event-count subtraction misleading. Convert each count to a risk: 30/200 = 15% and 10/100 = 10%. Their absolute difference is five percentage points, so NNT is 1/0.05 = 20 over three years. Remember: divide within groups before subtracting between groups, retaining the specified recurrence outcome and comparator.

decisionNodes.stem: For pneumothorax recurrence over five years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 20 percentage points; NNT 5 over five years
answerChoices.rationale: Subtract 10/100 from 30/100 to get 0.20. The reciprocal is 1/0.20 = 5 for the same comparator and five-year outcome.

answerChoices.label: ARR 67 percentage points; NNT 2 over five years
answerChoices.rationale: The risk falls by about two thirds relative to its starting value, but the absolute drop is 20 percentage points, not 67.

answerChoices.label: ARR 20 percentage points; NNT 50 over five years
answerChoices.rationale: The ARR is correct, but 1/0.20 is 5. An NNT of 50 is a reciprocal calculation error.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over five years
answerChoices.rationale: The two practice risks are 30% and 10%, a 20-point difference. A ten-point reduction would describe different inputs.

decisionNodes.explanation: The practice outcome risks differ by 0.30 - 0.10 = 0.20. ARR is 20 percentage points and NNT is 5 over the stated five-year period.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Absolute reduction subtracts risks on the same scale: 30% minus 10% is 20 percentage points. Taking the reciprocal of 0.20 gives NNT 5 for this comparator and outcome over five years. The relative reduction uses a different starting denominator. Remember that percentage points, percentages, and proportions are not interchangeable labels.

exhibit.caption: Unnamed investigational pleural device trial: invented practice counts of pneumothorax recurrence within five years. Cells count recurrences and people followed. Follow-up is complete; not real efficacy or personal risk.

answerChoices.label: ARR 14 percentage points; NNT 8 over two years

decisionNodes.stem: Which paired conclusion should {patientName} report from this study?

decisionNodes.stem: Which target-benefit conclusion and next study plan should {patientName}'s team report?

answerChoices.label: Target unresolved; plan a precision-focused efficacy study
answerChoices.rationale: The interval admits target-sized benefit as well as no benefit/harm. The target is unresolved despite a nonsignificant null test.

answerChoices.label: Target excluded; plan an alternative-intervention efficacy study
answerChoices.rationale: This treats nonsignificance as exclusion of the target-sized effects still in the interval.

answerChoices.label: Target confirmed; plan an implementation-feasibility study
answerChoices.rationale: This treats a favorable point estimate as satisfying the whole-interval target criterion.

decisionNodes.explanation: At the supplied two-sided threshold the null is not rejected. The interval contains effects meeting the target and effects failing it, so neither target confirmation nor target exclusion follows. A more precise efficacy estimate may resolve that uncertainty. Nonsignificance does not establish equivalence or futility, and the point estimate does not meet a whole-interval confirmation rule by itself.

decisionNodes.stem: Which testing error occurs in the simulated DCIS-recurrence analysis when the null is true but the analysis rejects it?

answerChoices.label: Type I error
answerChoices.rationale: The underlying null is stipulated to be true, yet the analysis rejects it. That truth-and-decision combination defines a type I error.

answerChoices.label: Type II error
answerChoices.rationale: Type II error would mean failing to reject under a specified true alternative. Both the underlying state and decision differ from this exhibit.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit gives the hypothesis state and decision, without describing inconsistent outcome measurement. It identifies a testing error rather than that bias mechanism.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias
answerChoices.rationale: No systematic exclusion from recruitment is supplied. The stated problem is rejection of a true null, not a selection process.

decisionNodes.explanation: Rejecting a true null is a type I error. The exhibit supplies the true state and testing decision, not evidence of a measurement or recruitment mechanism.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Testing errors compare a decision with the underlying state. Type I error means rejecting a null that is actually true; type II means failing to reject when a specified alternative is true. Here the null is true and was rejected. Remember: first identify what is true, then what the analysis decided.

decisionNodes.stem: What does prospective power describe under the specified alternative in the constructed pancreatic-cancer recurrence trial?

answerChoices.label: Chance of rejection if that alternative is true
answerChoices.rationale: Under the specified true alternative and design assumptions, power is the probability of rejecting the null. It describes how the planned procedure behaves in that situation.

answerChoices.label: Chance that a statistically positive result is true
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses what is conditioned on. Power assumes an alternative to evaluate rejection, rather than estimating whether a statistically positive conclusion is true.

answerChoices.label: Chance that the null hypothesis itself is true
answerChoices.rationale: The plan does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis being true. It calculates a rejection probability under the specified alternative.

answerChoices.label: Chance of nonrejection if that alternative is true
answerChoices.rationale: Nonrejection under a true alternative describes a type II error probability. Power instead concerns rejection under that alternative.

decisionNodes.explanation: Planned power is the chance of rejecting the null under the specified true alternative and design assumptions. It is not the truth probability of a positive result.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Power is the probability that the analysis rejects the null if the specified alternative is true, under the planned design assumptions. It is a statement about a procedure operating in that situation. Remember the direction of conditioning: it does not give the probability that a positive study conclusion or the alternative itself is true.

answerChoices.rationale: The later calculation does not make the no-effect conclusion valid. Neither low post-hoc power nor nonrejection supplies proof of an absent effect.

answerChoices.label: Post-hoc power gives the probability of the null
answerChoices.rationale: Power does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis. It concerns rejection behavior under a specified alternative.

answerChoices.label: The observed p-value is the study's achieved power
answerChoices.rationale: A p-value concerns observed-or-more-extreme data under a null model; power concerns rejection under an alternative. They are different conditional quantities.

decisionNodes.explanation: Low post-hoc power does not prove no effect. It neither gives the probability of the null nor makes the observed p-value equal to power.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Power describes rejection probability under a specified alternative, not the probability that a hypothesis is true. A low post-hoc power calculation after nonrejection does not establish an exactly absent effect. Remember that a second conditional calculation cannot transform the first result into proof of equality or supply the effect size missing from this exercise.

answerChoices.label: Adopt locally and plan the next test

answerChoices.label: Spread the change and monitor other clinics

answerChoices.label: Repeat the same pilot before making any change

answerChoices.label: Adapt the pathway before another local test
answerChoices.rationale: The findings identify no feature requiring revision before local adoption. Adaptation needs a reason in the learning, rather than a change for its own sake.

decisionNodes.explanation: Adopt the successful pathway locally and plan the next linked test. The favorable aim and balancing findings apply to the tested setting, not an untested wider rollout.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: The Act step turns learning into a decision and a next test. This pathway version met its aim without worsening the balancing measure, supporting local adoption and a linked next cycle. Keep the scope of action tied to the scope of the evidence: a successful small test does not automatically establish performance at every clinic.

decisionNodes.stem: Which Act-step decision fits the authorized venous-ulcer device pilot when healing is faster but application rework doubles?

answerChoices.label: Adapt device use and retest locally
answerChoices.rationale: Healing improved but rework doubled. Revise device use to address that burden and use the next test to study the adapted version.

answerChoices.label: Adopt device use and monitor application rework
answerChoices.rationale: Adopting this version unchanged accepts the documented worsening of rework. The balancing finding calls for adaptation before adoption.

answerChoices.label: Abandon device use and test another local idea
answerChoices.rationale: The target improvement supports retaining and adapting the idea. The supplied findings do not require discarding it instead of addressing the added burden.

answerChoices.label: Repeat device use without revising the process
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the same device unchanged does not respond to the increased rework already observed. The next cycle should use that learning.

decisionNodes.explanation: Adapt device use to address increased rework, then retest. The improved healing target supports keeping the idea, while the worsened balancing measure argues against adopting this version unchanged.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Improvement needs both the intended result and a check for shifted burden. This device shortened wound-closure time but doubled rework, so adapt its use and retest rather than adopting the current version unchanged. The Act step can preserve a promising idea while changing the part that caused trouble. Learning should change the next cycle.

cases.presentation: {patientName}, the hand-service improvement lead, reviews an authorized new wrist-bracing pathway for carpal tunnel syndrome. decisionNodes.stem: Which Act-step decision fits the authorized wrist-bracing pathway pilot when missing hand-function observations prevent judging its stated aim?

answerChoices.label: Fix data capture and repeat a bounded test
answerChoices.rationale: The missing observations prevent judging the aim. Repair data capture and repeat a bounded test so the next decision rests on interpretable results.

answerChoices.label: Adopt the change and improve later measurement
answerChoices.rationale: The incomplete records do not establish success. Adopting first and measuring later turns an information gap into an unsupported favorable verdict.

answerChoices.label: Adapt the intervention before collecting more data
answerChoices.rationale: The data gap does not identify an intervention feature to adapt. Fixing measurement addresses the known problem before choosing a specific revision.

answerChoices.label: Abandon the change and test a different idea
answerChoices.rationale: Incomplete measurement does not establish that the intervention failed. Abandonment would turn missing evidence into an unsupported unfavorable verdict.

decisionNodes.explanation: Fix data capture and repeat a bounded test. The missing observations prevent judging this intervention; they do not establish either success or failure.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: An uninterpretable test needs better measurement before an intervention verdict. Here missing observations prevent judging the aim, so repair data capture and repeat a bounded test. Remember the distinction between evidence of failure and failure to collect evidence; the latter does not establish adoption, adaptation, or abandonment of the intervention itself.

decisionNodes.stem: Which set lists a process measure, the intended clinical outcome measure and a balancing measure, in that order, for the ileostomy rehydration device pilot?

answerChoices.label: Device use as planned; dehydration episodes; application workload
answerChoices.rationale: Device use tracks implementation, dehydration episodes track the clinical aim, and application workload checks an unwanted tradeoff in delivering the intervention.

answerChoices.label: Dehydration episodes; device use as planned; application workload
answerChoices.rationale: Dehydration episodes measure the clinical outcome, while device use measures implementation. This ordering reverses process and outcome.

answerChoices.label: Device use as planned; application workload; dehydration episodes
answerChoices.rationale: Application workload checks a tradeoff, while dehydration episodes is the aim; this ordering swaps outcome and balancing measures.

answerChoices.rationale: Application workload belongs in the balancing position, while device use as planned belongs first; this ordering places both incorrectly.

decisionNodes.explanation: Device use tracks implementation, dehydration episodes track the clinical aim, and application workload checks a tradeoff. Counting applications alone does not establish a clinical improvement.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A process measure asks whether planned care happened; an outcome measure asks whether patients experienced the intended result. More device applications alone would not establish that dehydration improved.

decisionNodes.stem: Which set lists a process measure, the intended clinical outcome measure and a balancing measure, in that order, for the hidradenitis dressing device pilot?

answerChoices.label: Protocol dressing applications; time to lesion closure; extra application work
answerChoices.rationale: Applications track delivery, lesion-closure time tracks the healing aim, and extra application work checks the unwanted burden of delivering the new dressing.

answerChoices.label: Patients enrolled; protocol dressing applications; extra application work
answerChoices.rationale: Enrollment and application counts both track study or delivery activity. This set leaves out the clinical healing outcome the pilot intends to improve.

answerChoices.label: Protocol dressing applications; extra application work; time to lesion closure
answerChoices.rationale: Extra application work checks burden, not the healing aim. This ordering swaps the clinical outcome and balancing positions.

answerChoices.label: Time to lesion closure; extra application work; protocol dressing applications
answerChoices.rationale: Lesion-closure time is the clinical outcome, while applications track delivery. This ordering moves both outside their requested positions.

decisionNodes.explanation: Track dressing applications as process, lesion-closure time as outcome, and extra application work as balance. Enrollment and delivery counts cannot replace the intended clinical result.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A completed application is evidence of delivery, not evidence that a lesion closed sooner. Keep the clinical outcome separate from implementation counts, and check added work alongside both. Remember: doing the intervention and benefiting from it are different measurements. A balanced set can show whether better healing came with an application burden.

decisionNodes.stem: Which set lists a process measure, the intended clinical outcome measure and a balancing measure, in that order, for the lung-cancer screening program pilot?

answerChoices.label: Completed program screening; missed cancers at follow-up; extra diagnostic visits
answerChoices.rationale: Completed screening tracks delivery, missed cancers track the program’s diagnostic aim, and extra diagnostic visits check the additional assessment burden.

answerChoices.label: Screening invitations sent; screening visits completed; extra diagnostic visits

answerChoices.label: Completed program screening; extra diagnostic visits; missed cancers at follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Extra diagnostic visits check burden, while missed cancers measure the aim. This ordering swaps the outcome and balancing positions.

answerChoices.label: Missed cancers at follow-up; completed program screening; extra diagnostic visits
answerChoices.rationale: Missed cancers are the outcome and completed screening is process. This set places those two measures in the reverse order requested.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use completed program screening as process, missed cancers at follow-up as outcome, and extra diagnostic visits as balance. Attendance counts do not substitute for the diagnostic aim.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Screening activity and screening success need different measures. Completed screens track delivery; missed cancers at follow-up track the stated diagnostic aim; extra diagnostic visits check burden. Remember to count both what the program does and what it misses. decisionNodes.stem: Before discussing laparoscopic cholecystectomy for {patientName}'s symptomatic gallstones, what communication support is needed when patient and surgeon cannot communicate adequately?

answerChoices.label: Arrange qualified Spanish interpretation
answerChoices.rationale: Qualified Spanish interpretation supports an understandable discussion and the patient's own questions. Neither the child's offer nor the employee's bilingual skill establishes competence to interpret clinical information.

answerChoices.label: Use the child's interpretation for consent
answerChoices.rationale: The child wants to help, but willingness does not establish the competence needed for this clinical consent discussion. The patient still needs qualified interpretation.

answerChoices.label: Ask a bilingual clinic clerk to interpret
answerChoices.rationale: Speaking Spanish is not itself evidence of competence to interpret clinical information. The employee's qualification has not been established.

answerChoices.label: Use a translated Spanish consent handout
answerChoices.rationale: Written information can support the discussion, but cannot provide the qualified two-way exchange needed for the patient's own clinical questions.

decisionNodes.explanation: Arrange qualified Spanish interpretation so the patient can discuss the proposed cholecystectomy and ask questions. Neither the child's willingness nor the employee's bilingual conversation establishes interpreter competence.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Consent needs an understandable conversation, including the patient's own questions. When patient and clinician cannot communicate adequately, arrange qualified interpretation. A child's offer or an employee's conversational bilingual skill does not establish that competence. Make the conversation possible before asking for a decision; written materials can support, but cannot replace, that exchange.

decisionNodes.stem: With qualified interpretation in place, what is needed for informed consent to {patientName}'s laparoscopic cholecystectomy when material information has not been discussed?

answerChoices.label: Discuss risks, benefits, and alternatives
answerChoices.rationale: The patient lacks the clinical information needed to choose. Discuss the intervention's relevant risks, benefits, and alternatives, including foregoing it, in an understandable conversation.

answerChoices.label: Confirm the form was signed voluntarily
answerChoices.rationale: Voluntary signing matters, but confirming it does not supply the omitted risks, benefits, and alternatives. Information and voluntariness are separate needs.

answerChoices.label: Have the patient reread the consent document
answerChoices.rationale: Rereading the document does not by itself supply the clinical conversation that never occurred. A form can document consent without replacing the discussion.

answerChoices.label: Ask the patient to describe the planned operation
answerChoices.rationale: Describing the procedure's purpose checks only part of understanding. The stated gaps about relevant risks, benefits, and alternatives remain.

decisionNodes.explanation: The missing step is an understandable discussion of the intervention, risks, benefits, and alternatives. Confirming a signature or willingness alone does not fill those information gaps.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Informed consent helps a person understand the intervention, its relevant risks and benefits, and alternatives including declining, so the person can choose voluntarily. A signature cannot replace that conversation. The patient needs that discussion before the form can be relied on for the operation. Remember: document the conversation, rather than substituting a document for it.

decisionNodes.stem: What communication support is needed for {patientName}'s Graves-treatment discussion when the translation application leaves the patient's questions and answers unclear?

answerChoices.label: Arrange qualified medical interpretation
answerChoices.rationale: The app has left the patient's question about the Graves treatment unresolved. Qualified interpretation is needed to make the clinical exchange understandable before relying on consent.

answerChoices.label: Use the application's translated discussion
answerChoices.rationale: The application's output is already confusing and has not answered the patient's question. Reusing it does not establish an understandable exchange.

answerChoices.label: Ask a bilingual companion to interpret
answerChoices.rationale: A companion's language ability does not automatically establish qualified clinical interpretation. The patient's question needs an accurate, understandable exchange.

answerChoices.label: Provide translated written treatment information
answerChoices.rationale: A translated handout may support information, but it does not by itself resolve the patient's unanswered question through a two-way interpreted conversation.

decisionNodes.explanation: The application has left the treatment question unresolved. Arrange qualified interpretation before relying on the consent discussion; translated text alone does not establish that the exchange is understood.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A translation tool has not solved communication merely because it produces words. Here the patient's clinical question remains unclear, so qualified interpretation is needed for an understandable exchange. Remember the purpose: let the patient understand and ask questions before choosing. A companion or handout does not automatically supply that two-way clinical conversation.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: With qualified Spanish interpretation, {patientName}, a {patientAge}-year-old {patientSex}, has Graves disease and is considering surgery after discussing treatment goals. The patient can describe the proposed operation but has not heard the alternatives, including foregoing it. The clinic advertises a choice of appointments; both booking buttons lead to the same unavailable slot. The patient asks what other options exist.
decisionNodes.stem: With qualified interpretation in place, what information is missing before {patientName} can make an informed choice about surgery for Graves disease?

answerChoices.label: Discuss alternatives, including no procedure
answerChoices.rationale: The patient asks whether declining is an option. Discuss relevant alternatives and the implications of foregoing the operation, tailored to the situation.

answerChoices.label: Review the operation's expected diagnostic benefit
answerChoices.rationale: Expected diagnostic benefit is relevant, but repeating it leaves the question about declining and other options unanswered.

answerChoices.label: Review the operation's principal procedural risks
answerChoices.rationale: Procedural risks are relevant, but reviewing them alone still omits the alternatives and implications of no procedure that the patient is asking about.

answerChoices.label: Ask the patient to choose a surgical appointment
answerChoices.rationale: Choosing an appointment assumes the procedure decision is made. The patient still needs information about alternatives before making that choice.

decisionNodes.explanation: Discuss relevant alternatives, including no procedure and its implications. Repeating operation benefits or risks does not answer the patient's specific question about declining.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A decision is informed only if the patient can consider relevant alternatives, including foregoing the proposed intervention and what that would mean. Reviewing the procedure's benefits or risks alone leaves that question unanswered. Remember to explain the choice, not only the offered procedure, using an understandable conversation tailored to the patient's situation.

decisionNodes.stem: What communication support is needed for {patientName}'s skin-biopsy discussion when a relative answers but the patient's own questions remain unheard?

answerChoices.label: Arrange qualified Spanish interpretation
answerChoices.rationale: Qualified interpretation lets the patient speak and ask questions directly. The partner's answers cannot replace that participation when accurate independent communication is lacking.

answerChoices.label: Ask the partner to relay the patient's questions
answerChoices.rationale: The patient specifically wants to ask questions directly. Relying on the partner neither provides that exchange nor establishes qualified interpretation.

answerChoices.label: Ask a bilingual staff member to translate
answerChoices.rationale: Bilingual ability alone does not establish clinical interpreter competence. Another employee's language skills must not be treated as qualification by assumption.

answerChoices.label: Use a translated form for the patient's questions
answerChoices.rationale: A translated form cannot conduct the understandable two-way discussion the patient requests. Written support does not substitute for qualified interpretation.

decisionNodes.explanation: Arrange qualified Spanish interpretation for the patient's own questions. The partner's answers do not replace an understandable direct discussion, and bilingual ability alone does not establish interpreter competence.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Family participation can support a patient without replacing the patient's voice. When accurate communication is lacking, qualified interpretation lets the patient ask questions and make the decision directly. Remember to address the patient, not simply whoever speaks most. A partner's willingness or another employee's bilingual ability does not establish qualified clinical interpretation.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: With qualified Spanish interpretation, {patientName}, a {patientAge}-year-old {patientSex}, is discussing biopsy of a lesion suspicious for cutaneous SCC. After hearing the explanation, the patient says the procedure guarantees no scar. The presenter promises questions are welcome, then announces that questions ended on the previous slide. The biopsy has not started, and there is time to revisit the discussion.
decisionNodes.stem: With qualified interpretation in place, what should the team do when {patientName} mistakenly expects the skin biopsy to guarantee no scar?

answerChoices.label: Clarify scarring and ask for teach-back
answerChoices.rationale: The patient has demonstrated a specific misunderstanding about scarring. Clarify it, then ask the patient to explain the plan in their own words before relying on consent.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the explanation of the biopsy technique
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the biopsy technique does not necessarily address the supposed guarantee about scarring or check that the misunderstanding has been corrected.

answerChoices.label: Ask the patient to confirm willingness to proceed
answerChoices.rationale: Willingness to proceed is different from understanding the expected result. Confirming willingness leaves the demonstrated scarring misconception unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Review the signed consent form with the patient
answerChoices.rationale: Reviewing the form alone does not establish that the specific mistaken expectation has changed. Clarification and a check of understanding are needed.

decisionNodes.explanation: Clarify the mistaken scarring guarantee and ask for teach-back before relying on consent. Willingness or another reading of the form does not by itself establish corrected understanding.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A nod or signature does not settle a demonstrated misunderstanding. Clarify the mistaken expectation, then ask the patient to explain the plan in their own words to check understanding. Here the concern is a supposed guarantee about scarring. Remember: check what the patient understood, rather than assuming that hearing an explanation means understanding it.

decisionNodes.stem: What communication support is needed before {patientName} decides about esophageal manometry when the receptionist's limited Spanish cannot support the clinical discussion?

answerChoices.label: Arrange qualified medical interpretation
answerChoices.rationale: The receptionist is not qualified to interpret clinical information, and the clinician cannot support the full exchange. Arrange qualified interpretation for the patient's manometry questions and informed choice.

answerChoices.label: Use the receptionist's conversational Spanish
answerChoices.rationale: Knowing some phrases is not competence to interpret complex clinical information accurately and impartially. The supplied employee cannot fill that role.

answerChoices.label: Use an application to translate the discussion
answerChoices.rationale: The proposed app does not establish that this clinical consent conversation will be understood. The missing support is qualified interpretation.

answerChoices.label: Use a translated handout with written replies
answerChoices.rationale: Written exchanges do not establish an understandable clinical consent discussion or replace the qualified interpretation needed for the patient's questions.

decisionNodes.explanation: Arrange qualified interpretation for the clinical discussion. The receptionist is explicitly not qualified, and the proposed app or written exchanges do not establish the needed understandable conversation.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Knowing some phrases is different from interpreting clinical information accurately and impartially. This employee is not qualified for the discussion, so arrange qualified interpretation before relying on consent. Remember to assess whether the exchange is understandable, not whether someone can produce a translation. Written exchanges and apps do not establish that missing competence here.

decisionNodes.currentUpdate: With qualified Spanish interpretation, {patientName}, a {patientAge}-year-old {patientSex}, is discussing nonurgent manometry for suspected achalasia after structural obstruction was excluded. Information has been provided, but a companion threatens to withhold transportation unless the patient signs. In private, the patient says the study is unwanted. Testing has not started, and there is time to discuss the patient's own choice.
decisionNodes.stem: With qualified interpretation in place, how should the team respond when {patientName} privately declines nonurgent manometry after a companion threatens to withhold transportation unless the patient signs?

answerChoices.label: Pause and support the patient's voluntary choice
answerChoices.rationale: The patient privately says the procedure is unwanted after a threat about transport. Pause the elective process and support a voluntary choice rather than rely on the pressured signature.

answerChoices.label: Ask the patient to confirm consent with the companion
answerChoices.rationale: Asking for confirmation in the companion's presence preserves the setting of pressure. It does not protect the voluntary choice expressed in private.

answerChoices.label: Offer another appointment with the same companion
answerChoices.rationale: A later appointment with the same companion does not itself address the pressure undermining consent. Changing the date is not a voluntariness assessment.

answerChoices.label: Ask the companion to explain the patient's preferences
answerChoices.rationale: The companion's account cannot replace the patient's private expressed preference. Practical support does not give the companion authority to impose the elective choice.

decisionNodes.explanation: Pause and support the patient's voluntary choice. The private refusal and companion's threat undermine reliance on a pressured signature for an nonurgent study with no urgent need.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Consent requires a voluntary choice as well as information and understanding. A signature obtained under the pressure described here cannot substitute for the patient's expressed preference. Pause the nonurgent process and support a voluntary decision in private. Remember that a companion's wishes do not become the patient's wishes merely because the companion provides practical support.

decisionNodes.stem: How should the team respond to {patientName}'s informed refusal of appendectomy when the stated decision-making abilities are intact?

answerChoices.label: Respect refusal and discuss follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: The patient demonstrates informed understanding, coherent reasoning, and a consistent refusal. Respect that choice and discuss follow-up; surgeon disagreement does not establish incapacity.

answerChoices.label: Request psychiatric clearance before accepting refusal
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied concern is disagreement, not inability to decide. That alone does not establish a need for psychiatric clearance before accepting an informed refusal.

answerChoices.label: Ask the family to confirm the treatment decision
answerChoices.rationale: The patient's demonstrated abilities support making this decision. Family agreement is not what validates this capable adult's informed refusal.

answerChoices.label: Repeat consent counseling until surgery is accepted
answerChoices.rationale: Further counseling can address an unanswered question, but repeating it until agreement replaces the informed choice already demonstrated in this scenario.

decisionNodes.explanation: Respect the informed refusal and discuss follow-up. The patient demonstrates the required abilities; the surgeon's disagreement alone does not justify replacing the decision or requiring psychiatric or family approval.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Capacity concerns the decision in front of you and the patient's demonstrated abilities, not agreement with the clinician. This patient understands the options and personal implications, reasons coherently, and communicates a consistent refusal. Respect that informed choice and discuss follow-up. Remember: a recommendation can be reasonable without making disagreement evidence of incapacity.

decisionNodes.stem: What should the team do before elective parathyroid surgery when {patientName} is newly confused and cannot understand the operation despite an earlier consent signature?

answerChoices.label: Pause and assess capacity for this decision
answerChoices.rationale: New confusion, inability to explain the purpose, and changing answers raise present capacity concerns. Pause and assess this decision before the elective intervention.

answerChoices.label: Verify the earlier consent and continue preparation
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier signature records an earlier discussion. It does not resolve the patient's new inability to understand the current decision.

answerChoices.label: Obtain a fresh signature after repeating the explanation
answerChoices.rationale: A fresh signature after another repetition does not establish understanding. The patient's present abilities need assessment rather than replacement documentation.

answerChoices.label: Ask a relative to approve the procedure first
answerChoices.rationale: A relative's approval first bypasses assessment of the patient's current decision-making abilities. Address the present concern before assuming someone else should decide.

decisionNodes.explanation: Pause the elective process and assess capacity for the current decision. The earlier form does not resolve new confusion and inability to explain the procedure's purpose.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Capacity can change, so an earlier signature does not answer a present concern about understanding. New confusion and inability to explain this procedure warrant pausing and assessing the current decision. Remember to assess the person now for this choice. A fresh signature or a relative's approval does not replace addressing that concern.

decisionNodes.stem: How should the team assess {patientName}'s refusal of thyroid needle sampling when treated depression is recorded but the stated decision-making abilities are intact?

answerChoices.label: Assess current decision-making abilities
answerChoices.rationale: Assess the demonstrated abilities for this specific decision. Accurate understanding, personal appreciation, coherent reasoning, and a stable choice cannot be dismissed because depression is recorded.

answerChoices.label: Require psychiatric clearance because of depression
answerChoices.rationale: Depression alone does not establish incapacity or a requirement for psychiatric clearance. The actual abilities demonstrated in this discussion matter.

answerChoices.label: Use the family's account of the patient's usual judgment
answerChoices.rationale: Family observations can provide context, but a description of usual judgment does not replace assessing the patient's present abilities for this decision.

answerChoices.label: Judge capacity by agreement with the recommendation
answerChoices.rationale: Agreement with the clinician is not a capacity criterion. A reasoned refusal can demonstrate the required abilities even when the clinician favors revision.

decisionNodes.explanation: Judge current abilities for this decision, not depression alone. The patient demonstrates understanding, appreciation, coherent reasoning, and a stable choice, supporting respect for the refusal.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A diagnosis is not a capacity verdict. Assess understanding, personal appreciation, reasoning, and communication for the actual decision. The described abilities support respecting this refusal despite the history of depression. Remember to examine what the patient can do in this discussion, rather than replacing an individual assessment with a diagnostic label or agreement test.
sourceLabels: Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity

decisionNodes.stem: How should the team approach {patientName}'s decision about a varicose-vein intervention when mild cognitive impairment is recorded but supported understanding is demonstrated?

answerChoices.label: Support and assess the patient's own decision
answerChoices.rationale: Support understanding and assess the patient's own abilities for vein intervention. The described informed, consistent choice should not be displaced solely by the cognitive diagnosis.

answerChoices.label: Obtain a surrogate's decision because of the diagnosis
answerChoices.rationale: Cognitive impairment does not eliminate capacity for every decision. Seeking a surrogate solely from that label skips the abilities demonstrated after support.

answerChoices.label: Require a family countersignature for this consent
answerChoices.rationale: A family countersignature does not replace assessing the patient's supported understanding and choice. The diagnosis alone does not establish that another person must validate consent.

answerChoices.label: Require formal testing before discussing the choice
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied discussion already demonstrates relevant abilities with support. A blanket testing requirement based on the diagnosis does not address those actual abilities.

decisionNodes.explanation: Support and assess the patient's own decision about treatment. Demonstrated understanding after plain-language explanation cannot be dismissed solely because cognitive impairment is recorded.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Cognitive impairment does not remove capacity for every decision. Support understanding and assess the patient's actual abilities for this choice before seeking a substitute decision-maker. Plain language enables an informed, consistent choice. Remember that the diagnosis and the decision are separate questions; a label alone does not transfer authority to family or a surrogate.
sourceLabels: Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity

answerChoices.label: Continue current self-care alone
answerChoices.rationale: Persistent symptoms and treatment preference merit referral.

answerChoices.label: Start anticoagulation
answerChoices.rationale: Reflux without thrombosis is not an indication for anticoagulation.

decisionNodes.stem: What should guide the authorized surrogate's operative decision for {patientName}'s acute cholecystitis when known patient wishes differ from the surrogate's own preference?

answerChoices.label: Use the patient's known preferences
answerChoices.rationale: Specific prior discussions identify what this patient would choose in these circumstances. Substituted judgment uses those known wishes rather than the surrogate's own preference.

answerChoices.label: Use the surrogate's preferred treatment plan
answerChoices.rationale: The surrogate represents the patient's known perspective. Personally favoring treatment does not justify replacing the patient's specific contrary wishes.

answerChoices.label: Use the family's agreed treatment preference
answerChoices.rationale: Family agreement does not displace a known patient preference. Counting relatives' choices answers whose plan is popular, rather than what this patient would choose.

answerChoices.label: Use the option with the greatest expected benefit
answerChoices.rationale: Best-interest deliberation is the fallback when wishes cannot be determined. Here known preferences supply the patient's perspective rather than leaving it unknown.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use the patient's known preferences through substituted judgment. The surrogate's own preference does not replace specific prior wishes about these circumstances.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Substituted judgment asks what this patient would choose, using known preferences and values. It does not ask what the surrogate would choose for themselves or what most relatives prefer. Here specific prior wishes are available. Remember that the surrogate represents the patient's perspective; best-interest deliberation is the fallback when that perspective cannot be determined.
sourceLabels: Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity

decisionNodes.stem: What should guide the authorized surrogate's rectal-prolapse surgical deliberation for {patientName} when prior wishes and relevant values cannot be determined?

answerChoices.label: The patient's benefits and burdens
answerChoices.rationale: The patient's wishes and values remain unknown after reasonable efforts. Best-interest deliberation therefore weighs likely benefits, burdens, and suffering for the patient.

answerChoices.label: The choice most family members would make
answerChoices.rationale: A family majority does not establish the patient's best interests. The supplied standard requires attention to the patient's benefits and burdens.

answerChoices.label: The option with the longest possible survival
answerChoices.rationale: Possible survival is one consideration, not a complete substitute for weighing benefits, burdens, and suffering. The standard is broader than maximizing duration alone.

answerChoices.label: The surrogate's preferred treatment for themself
answerChoices.rationale: The surrogate's own treatment preference is not the patient's known preference or a complete assessment of the patient's welfare.

decisionNodes.explanation: Use the patient's best interests, weighing benefits and burdens. No prior preferences can be identified, so neither family voting nor the surrogate's personal treatment preference supplies the standard.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: When the patient's preferences and values cannot be determined, consider the patient's best interests, including likely benefits, burdens, and suffering. This differs from substituting the surrogate's personal choice or counting family votes. Remember to look for the patient's perspective first; when it is unavailable, keep the patient's welfare at the center of deliberation.
sourceLabels: Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity
Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Rectal Prolapse

decisionNodes.stem: What is the appropriate next step when the surrogate's requested kidney-stone evaluation conflicts with {patientName}'s documented wishes and discussion has not resolved the disagreement?

answerChoices.label: Seek ethics support for the conflict
answerChoices.rationale: The request still conflicts with documented wishes despite discussion. Appropriate institutional ethics support addresses that unresolved conflict instead of accepting the surrogate's request automatically.

answerChoices.label: Ask another relative to approve the requested treatment
answerChoices.rationale: Another relative's agreement does not resolve the conflict with the patient's documented wishes. Changing who endorses the plan leaves the same ethical concern.

answerChoices.label: Use the surrogate's current request as the final decision
answerChoices.rationale: An authorized surrogate's request is not automatic permission to disregard known patient wishes. The unresolved disagreement calls for appropriate support.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the same family meeting before seeking advice
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied discussion has already failed to resolve the conflict. Repeating it unchanged is not a substitute for seeking the appropriate institutional ethics support.

decisionNodes.explanation: Seek appropriate institutional ethics support for the unresolved conflict. The surrogate's request remains inconsistent with documented wishes, and there is time to address it without automatic compliance.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: A surrogate request does not automatically override known patient wishes. When discussion leaves that conflict unresolved, appropriate institutional ethics support can help address it rather than accepting the request by default. Remember to preserve the patient's perspective during disagreement. Substituting a different relative or repeating an unchanged meeting does not itself resolve the ethical conflict.
sourceLabels: Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity

decisionNodes.stem: How should {patientName} participate in the neck-mass sampling discussion when a surrogate must make the complex decision but the patient can express concerns and preferences?

answerChoices.label: Include the patient as abilities allow
answerChoices.rationale: The patient retains abilities to express concerns and preferences. Include that participation while the authorized surrogate handles the complex choice requiring substitute authority.

answerChoices.label: Ask the surrogate to relay the patient's concerns
answerChoices.rationale: Relying only on the surrogate to relay concerns omits the direct participation the patient can still provide. Needing a surrogate does not require that exclusion.

answerChoices.label: Limit discussion to the surrogate's treatment choice
answerChoices.rationale: Limiting discussion to the surrogate's choice ignores the patient's remaining abilities and expressed comfort concerns. Those views still deserve attention.

answerChoices.label: Use the patient's simple preference as the final decision
answerChoices.rationale: A simple preference can inform deliberation without establishing capacity for the complex decision. Participation should not be mistaken for complete final authority.

decisionNodes.explanation: Include the patient as abilities allow, while the surrogate makes the complex decision. Remaining comfort concerns and simple preferences still deserve direct attention.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Needing a surrogate for one complex choice does not erase every ability to participate. Include the patient to the extent possible and attend to expressed comfort concerns and preferences, while the surrogate handles the complex decision. Remember that participation and final decision authority are separate; neither exclusion nor substitution of a simple preference fits here.
sourceLabels: Decisions for Adult Patients Who Lack Capacity
Head and Neck Cancer: United Kingdom National Multidisciplinary Guidelines, Sixth Edition

decisionNodes.stem: How should the team address {patientName}'s existing DNR order before elective inguinal-hernia repair when the checklist proposes automatic suspension?

answerChoices.label: Discuss and document the patient's preferences
answerChoices.rationale: Individualized discussion with the patient or surrogate and responsible clinicians establishes and documents preferences for the operative context. The checklist cannot make that decision automatically.

answerChoices.label: Use the operating room's usual resuscitation plan
answerChoices.rationale: A standard operating-room plan does not substitute for reviewing this patient's preferences. It bypasses the individualized discussion required here.

answerChoices.label: Carry the existing order forward without reconsideration
answerChoices.rationale: Leaving the order unchanged without reconsideration skips review of how it applies to the proposed operation and anesthesia. Individualization is needed rather than an automatic default.

answerChoices.label: Suspend the order while obtaining routine surgical consent
answerChoices.rationale: Suspending first and obtaining routine consent does not replace an individualized resuscitation discussion. An automatic suspension bypasses the patient's preferences.

decisionNodes.explanation: Discuss and document an individualized resuscitation plan with the patient or surrogate and responsible clinicians. An automatic operating-room rule does not replace that review.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Perioperative DNR planning requires an individualized review with the patient or surrogate and responsible clinicians. Automatically suspending the order bypasses that discussion; carrying it forward without reconsideration also leaves the operative context unexplored. Remember to discuss and document the patient's preferences rather than treating entry to the operating room as the decision itself.
sourceLabels: Statement on Ethical Guidelines for the Anesthesia Care of Patients with Do-Not-Resuscitate Orders
International guidelines for groin hernia management

decisionNodes.stem: What should the anesthesia team clarify and document with {patientName} before gastrectomy when an existing DNR order raises questions about perioperative interventions?

answerChoices.label: Clarify feasible limits and document the plan
answerChoices.rationale: Clarify requested limits, procedures essential to the proposed anesthesia, and an agreed documented plan. That answers the patient's practical questions before the operation.

answerChoices.label: Carry the current limits into the anesthetic plan
answerChoices.rationale: Carrying limits forward without discussion does not clarify their application to anesthesia or the interventions essential to the proposed care.

answerChoices.label: Use a procedure-specific standard resuscitation plan
answerChoices.rationale: A procedure-specific standard is still a generic plan. It does not resolve this patient's requested limits through individualized discussion.

answerChoices.label: Leave decisions to the anesthetist during the operation
answerChoices.rationale: Waiting for decisions during the operation leaves the supplied questions unresolved beforehand. Clarification and agreement belong in the planned discussion.

decisionNodes.explanation: Clarify feasible limits, essential anesthetic procedures, and an agreed documented plan. Leaving the issue until the operation or using a generic policy does not resolve the patient's questions beforehand.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Requested limits need discussion in the context of anesthesia. Clarify the interventions, identify what is essential to planned care, and document an agreed individualized plan with the patient or surrogate and responsible clinicians. Remember that neither a generic procedure policy nor an unchanged order answers every practical question about how those limits apply.

decisionNodes.stem: What must the team add to {patientName}'s ileal-resection plan after agreeing on temporary perioperative changes to an existing DNR order?

answerChoices.label: The time for resuming the original limits
answerChoices.rationale: The temporary change needs a documented endpoint for reinstating the original directive. That is the omitted detail identified in this note.

answerChoices.label: The clinician authorizing the temporary change
answerChoices.rationale: Identifying an authorizing clinician does not say when the original limits resume. The missing endpoint remains unresolved.

answerChoices.label: The interventions permitted during anesthesia
answerChoices.rationale: Permitted interventions are already recorded. Repeating them would not supply the omitted timing or condition for reinstatement.

answerChoices.label: The surrogate confirming the operative goals
answerChoices.rationale: The operative goals are already documented. Surrogate confirmation of those goals does not itself establish when the prior limits return.

decisionNodes.explanation: Document when the original limits will resume. The note already describes the temporary intervention permissions and goals, but a modification without an endpoint can remain ambiguous.
decisionNodes.teachingPoint: Temporary modification needs a documented endpoint for reinstating the original directive. Recording the permitted interventions alone leaves uncertainty about when the earlier limits resume. Remember to plan both the change and its end with the responsible team. This question asks for that missing endpoint, not a universal time that applies to every operation.

decisionNodes.stem: Which directive order should be communicated at that handover for {patientName}?

answerChoices.label: Reinstate DNR while oxygen continues
answerChoices.rationale: The agreed endpoint is return to baseline, not independence from a treatment that was already necessary before anaesthesia. Prescribed baseline oxygen continues under the separately agreed care plan.

answerChoices.label: Reinstate DNR after oxygen discontinuation
answerChoices.rationale: This confuses chronic preoperative support with an unresolved acute anaesthetic effect and would extend the modification beyond the stipulated reassessed endpoint.

answerChoices.label: Reinstate DNR after usual activity returns
answerChoices.rationale: Mobility recovery can matter to discharge, but it is not the cardiopulmonary endpoint agreed for this directive.

decisionNodes.explanation: The temporary modification has the endpoint agreed with the patient: reassessed return to the pre-anaesthetic cardiopulmonary condition. Baseline prescribed oxygen does not make that endpoint unmet. Reinstate the original directive and continue other treatment consistent with the separate care plan. Neither stopping chronic oxygen nor waiting for functional recovery was agreed as the endpoint.

decisionNodes.stem: Which treatment should the team arrange for {patientName}'s clinically evident, uncomplicated superficial perianal abscess when the patient wants treatment and the DNR order remains in place?

answerChoices.label: Arrange incision and drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Arrange prompt incision and drainage for this clinically evident superficial perianal abscess rather than delaying source control.

answerChoices.label: Arrange an oral antibiotic course
answerChoices.rationale: Antibiotics alone do not provide source control for a drainable abscess.

answerChoices.label: Arrange warm-compress treatment
answerChoices.rationale: Supportive measures alone do not replace drainage of this evident collection.

answerChoices.label: Arrange aspiration through a needle
answerChoices.rationale: Needle aspiration alone is not the standard source-control procedure for a routine perianal abscess.

decisionNodes.explanation: Arrange prompt incision and drainage for the evident superficial perianal collection. Antibiotics, compresses or needle aspiration alone do not replace the authored drainage plan.
