question.statistics-ethics.study-design..patientPresentation: {patientName}, the foregut journal-club lead, reviews a new wearable test for reflux disease. A survey records device use and current reflux symptoms at one visit, without allocating treatment or following participants afterward. The author calls the questionnaire streamlined; its optional feedback section first requires an explanation of why the feedback is optional. Recruitment details accompany the report.
question.statistics-ethics.study-design..stem: Which study design matches how the investigators selected participants, handled the study intervention and measured the clinical outcome described in the exhibit?

answerChoices.label: Cross-sectional study
answerChoices.rationale: Current device use and reflux symptoms are recorded together, without outcome-based recruitment or follow-up. Those features define this cross-sectional snapshot.

answerChoices.label: Case-control study
answerChoices.rationale: Case-control recruitment would depend on outcome status. The exhibit explicitly says recruitment does not depend on the current symptom findings.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Case-control recruitment would depend on outcome status. The exhibit explicitly says recruitment does not depend on the current symptom findings.

answerChoices.label: Prospective cohort study
answerChoices.rationale: A prospective cohort would organize exposure groups and observe later outcomes. This survey has no follow-up after the same-visit measurements.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A prospective cohort would organize exposure groups and observe later outcomes. This survey has no follow-up after the same-visit measurements.

answerChoices.label: Randomized experiment
answerChoices.rationale: A randomized experiment requires investigator assignment. This survey records device use and symptoms without assigning a device or study arm.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A randomized experiment requires investigator assignment. This survey records device use and symptoms without assigning a device or study arm.

question.statistics-ethics.study-design..explanation: This is a cross-sectional survey: device use and current reflux symptoms were recorded together, without outcome-based recruitment, subsequent follow-up or investigator-assigned intervention.
question.statistics-ethics.study-design..teachingPoint: A cross-sectional study records exposure and outcome at one time, giving a snapshot. Here device use and current symptoms are measured together, without outcome-based recruitment, assignment or follow-up. Remember what the study actually observed. A report title cannot create a time sequence or treatment allocation that the design never supplied.

exhibit.title: Reflux findings — illustrative study design
exhibit.body: A survey records use of a new wearable reflux test and current reflux symptoms at the same visit. Recruitment is not based on symptom status; there is no follow-up or allocation. This unnamed investigational wearable reflux test protocol is invented for practice, not an actual study or efficacy estimate.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the abdominal-wall research lead, reviews a new reinforcement material for incisional hernia repair. The observational study compares recurrence within two years. The sponsor wants a clean comparison, meaning a report without complicated caveats. The exhibit describes a study site related to both material use and recurrence; the unadjusted report does not account for that site.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.stem: Which problem most directly threatens the unadjusted intervention-outcome comparison when study site relates to both?

answerChoices.label: Confounding by study site
answerChoices.rationale: Site relates to both intervention use and the outcome, and the comparison ignores it. Their mixed association is the stated confounding concern.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit describes an ignored third factor in the comparison, not differential entry into the sample. That is the confounding rather than selection mechanism supplied.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit describes an ignored third factor in the comparison, not differential entry into the sample. That is the confounding rather than selection mechanism supplied.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from recall
answerChoices.rationale: No unequal recall or outcome-recording method is described. The stated problem is the ignored relationship of site with both exposure and outcome.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No unequal recall or outcome-recording method is described. The stated problem is the ignored relationship of site with both exposure and outcome.

answerChoices.label: Random error from sample size
answerChoices.rationale: More observations do not automatically remove the systematic mixing with site. Sample-size variation is not the primary mechanism described.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: More observations do not automatically remove the systematic mixing with site. Sample-size variation is not the primary mechanism described.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.explanation: Study site is a confounder in this exercise because it relates to both intervention use and the outcome and is ignored in the comparison.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.teachingPoint: Confounding occurs when an exposure comparison is mixed with another associated factor. Here site relates to both intervention use and the outcome, so the unadjusted association may combine those relationships. Remember the third-factor question: what else differs with exposure and outcome? More observations do not automatically remove that systematic problem.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational hernia reinforcement material study: Study site predicts both material use and two-year hernia recurrence. The unadjusted comparison ignores site; that relationship is stipulated for this exercise, not a clinical risk-factor claim. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the neck-surgery journal-club lead, reviews a new dissection technique for symptomatic thyroglossal duct cysts. Investigators record surgical-site infection within thirty days. The author says every patient's voice matters; recruitment stopped whenever the coordinator went home. The report presents its conclusion as applying to all eligible patients, although enrollment covered daytime operations and excluded nighttime operations.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.stem: Which bias most directly limits the claim about all eligible surgical patients when recruitment covers daytime operations only?

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from daytime-only recruitment
answerChoices.rationale: Daytime encounters alone are used to make an all-patients claim. The missing nighttime surgical patients create the stated selection concern even with a large daytime sample.

answerChoices.label: Confounding by an unmeasured patient characteristic
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied mechanism is who entered the audit. No patient factor relating both exposure and outcome is identified as the primary concern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supplied mechanism is who entered the audit. No patient factor relating both exposure and outcome is identified as the primary concern.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from unequal recall windows
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit does not describe unequal recall. It describes exclusion of nighttime surgical patients from an all-patients conclusion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit does not describe unequal recall. It describes exclusion of nighttime surgical patients from an all-patients conclusion.

answerChoices.label: Random error from insufficient sample precision
answerChoices.rationale: A large daytime sample can still exclude the target population of nighttime surgical patients. Greater sampling precision does not repair that selection problem.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A large daytime sample can still exclude the target population of nighttime surgical patients. Greater sampling precision does not repair that selection problem.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.explanation: Daytime-only sampling creates the stated selection concern. Adding more daytime surgical patients does not supply the missing nighttime surgical observations needed for the all-patients conclusion.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.teachingPoint: Selection bias concerns which observations enter the study. A large daytime-only sample still leaves nighttime surgical patients outside an audit presented as applying to all eligible surgical patients. Sample size cannot repair that missing coverage. Distinguish this selection problem from confounding within the comparison or inconsistent measurement after people have entered it.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational thyroglossal-cyst dissection technique study: Investigators enroll daytime operations and no nighttime operations, yet present their thirty-day SSI conclusion as applying to all eligible surgical patients. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

agentReview.scope: Technical, editorial, source-traceability, and internal-consistency review; named clinician review remains required.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the perioperative research lead, reviews a new calf-stimulation device and postoperative DVT. One group reported thrombotic events when they occurred; another recalled events six months later. A colleague points out that everyone used the same form. The investigators are reviewing the collection process, and the report specifies how the two reporting schedules differed during follow-up.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.stem: Which information problem most directly threatens the outcome comparison when one group reports immediately and the other recalls events six months later?

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from unequal recall
answerChoices.rationale: Immediate recording in one group and recall six months later in the other use unequal measurement processes. That can systematically distort the recorded contrast.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: The difference concerns how outcomes were recorded after entry, rather than how people were selected for the study.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The difference concerns how outcomes were recorded after entry, rather than how people were selected for the study.

answerChoices.label: Confounding by baseline study site
answerChoices.rationale: No baseline site factor is supplied as relating exposure and the outcome. The stated concern is the unequal reporting schedule.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No baseline site factor is supplied as relating exposure and the outcome. The stated concern is the unequal reporting schedule.

answerChoices.label: Random error from natural variation
answerChoices.rationale: The groups are measured by different recall processes. That systematic difference is not simply random variation that a larger sample necessarily removes.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The groups are measured by different recall processes. That systematic difference is not simply random variation that a larger sample necessarily removes.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.explanation: The primary concern is measurement bias from unequal recall schedules. The groups' recorded outcomes may differ because one reports immediately and the other recalls much later.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.teachingPoint: Measurement bias can arise when groups' outcomes are recorded differently. Immediate reports and recall six months later use unequal measurement processes, so a difference in reports may reflect how the outcomes were remembered. This is distinct from who was recruited or which baseline factor confounds the comparison. Larger samples do not equalize the reporting methods.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational calf-stimulation device study: One group reports postoperative DVT events immediately; the other recalls those events six months later. The reporting schedules differ; no real device effect is supplied. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

agentReview.scope: Technical, editorial, source-traceability, and internal-consistency review; named clinician review remains required.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the anesthesia journal-club lead, reviews a new monitoring sensor for malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility. An observational model compares recognition of concerning intraoperative changes. Investigators adjusted for recorded differences between groups. Follow-up access relates to both sensor choice and recorded recognition, but important access differences were not measured. The report describes those stipulated relationships and the model under review.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.stem: Which limitation remains after adjustment when an important factor related to both sensor choice and recorded outcomes was not measured?

answerChoices.label: Residual confounding by unmeasured factors
answerChoices.rationale: Unrecorded follow-up access differences relate to intervention choice and the outcome. Adjustment for other factors leaves that potential confounding unresolved.

answerChoices.label: Random error from the sampling process
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit identifies an unrecorded associated factor, not just sampling variability. Greater precision would not supply the missing follow-up access information.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit identifies an unrecorded associated factor, not just sampling variability. Greater precision would not supply the missing follow-up access information.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias from study enrollment
answerChoices.rationale: No enrollment mechanism is described as the primary concern. The known limitation is confounding by follow-up access differences absent from the model.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No enrollment mechanism is described as the primary concern. The known limitation is confounding by follow-up access differences absent from the model.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias from inconsistent outcome recording
answerChoices.rationale: No inconsistent outcome-recording process is supplied. The gap is a relevant factor the model could not adjust for because it was not recorded.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No inconsistent outcome-recording process is supplied. The gap is a relevant factor the model could not adjust for because it was not recorded.

question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.explanation: Residual confounding remains because relevant follow-up access differences were not measured. Adjusting for site and procedure category does not automatically account for that unrecorded factor.
question.statistics-ethics.bias-confound.teachingPoint: Adjustment can address recorded factors without accounting for unrecorded ones. Follow-up access still relates to both intervention choice and the outcome, so residual confounding remains possible despite adjustment for site and procedure category. Remember that an adjusted label is not a guarantee of an unconfounded result; ask which relevant differences the model could actually use.

exhibit.title: Clinical study — illustrative bias review
exhibit.body: An unnamed investigational anesthesia monitoring sensor study: The model adjusts for measured site and procedure category. Follow-up access relates to both sensor choice and recorded recognition of concerning intraoperative changes, but important access differences were not recorded. These relationships are stipulated, not general clinical risk-factor claims. These study conditions are invented for practice, not real intervention results.

question.statistics-ethics.sensitivity-s.explanation: Use the condition-present row: 90/(90 + 10) = 90% sensitivity. The positive-result column answers a different question, and this practice table is not a personal risk estimate.
question.statistics-ethics.sensitivity-s.teachingPoint: Sensitivity starts with people who have the condition by the reference assessment: how many tested positive? Here 90 of 100 did, giving 90%. question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.stem: How does the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's positive predictive value change between the hypothetical populations when sensitivity and specificity remain fixed as stated?

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value increases
answerChoices.rationale: With sensitivity and specificity fixed, the higher-prevalence population has a greater true-positive share among positive screens. This supports an increase, without an exact percentage.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value decreases
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction: higher prevalence increases the true-positive share among positives under the fixed-test assumptions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the direction: higher prevalence increases the true-positive share among positives under the fixed-test assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value stays fixed
answerChoices.rationale: Fixed sensitivity and specificity do not fix positive predictive value. Prevalence also determines the mix of true and false positives.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Fixed sensitivity and specificity do not fix positive predictive value. Prevalence also determines the mix of true and false positives.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value is indeterminate
answerChoices.rationale: An exact percentage would need more numbers, but the direction follows from higher prevalence with fixed test characteristics. That direction is not indeterminate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An exact percentage would need more numbers, but the direction follows from higher prevalence with fixed test characteristics. That direction is not indeterminate.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.explanation: Positive predictive value increases under the stated fixed-test assumptions because prevalence is higher. The exhibit supports the direction of change without supplying an exact personal probability.
question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.teachingPoint: Positive predictive value asks what share of positive results come from people with the condition. With sensitivity and specificity held fixed, higher prevalence makes true positives a larger share of positives, so predictive value rises. Remember that the test and the tested population both matter; this comparison gives direction, not a personal percentage.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.stem: How does the new investigational breast-cancer blood test's positive predictive value change between the hypothetical populations when sensitivity and specificity remain fixed as stated?

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value decreases
answerChoices.rationale: With sensitivity and specificity fixed, lower prevalence means false positives form a larger share of positive screens. Positive predictive value therefore decreases.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value increases
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the stated comparison. Lower prevalence decreases the true-positive share among positive screens under these fixed-test assumptions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the stated comparison. Lower prevalence decreases the true-positive share among positive screens under these fixed-test assumptions.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value stays fixed
answerChoices.rationale: Two populations can have the same test characteristics but different predictive values because prevalence differs.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Two populations can have the same test characteristics but different predictive values because prevalence differs.

answerChoices.label: Positive predictive value is indeterminate
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit lacks an exact percentage, but still establishes a decrease under the lower-prevalence, fixed-test assumptions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit lacks an exact percentage, but still establishes a decrease under the lower-prevalence, fixed-test assumptions.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.teachingPoint: A test's positive predictive value depends on the population as well as its sensitivity and specificity. With those test characteristics fixed, lower prevalence makes false positives a larger share of positive screens, so predictive value falls. A fixed test is not a fixed predictive value; the exhibit establishes direction without an exact percentage.

answerChoices.rationale: Start with all positive screens: 40 + 10 = 50. Forty had the condition, so positive predictive value is 40/50 = 80%.
The calculation 30/(10 + 30) = 75% uses the condition-absent row. It answers a specificity question, not the positive-screen question asked.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The calculation 30/(10 + 30) = 75% uses the condition-absent row. It answers a specificity question, not the positive-screen question asked.

answerChoices.rationale: The calculation 10/(40 + 10) = 20% is the false-positive share among positives. The requested predictive value counts true positives instead.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The calculation 10/(40 + 10) = 20% is the false-positive share among positives. The requested predictive value counts true positives instead.

answerChoices.rationale: The calculation 40/(40 + 20) is about 67%. It begins with people who have the condition and therefore calculates sensitivity.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The calculation 40/(40 + 20) is about 67%. It begins with people who have the condition and therefore calculates sensitivity.

question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.explanation: Read the positive-screen column: 40 true positives and 10 false positives. Positive predictive value is 40/50 = 80% for these practice data.
question.statistics-ethics.predictive-va.teachingPoint: Positive predictive value asks, of all positive results, how many were true positives? Its denominator includes true and false positives. Here 40 of 50 positives had the condition, giving 80%. Sensitivity instead starts with people known to have the condition. Remember which group the question starts with before choosing a row or column.

answerChoices.label: Different prevalence in the tested populations

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the biliary journal-club lead, reviews a new dissection instrument for acute cholecystitis operations. The observational study reports surgical-site infection within thirty days. Its sponsor requests a balanced account: equal space for the data and the company's response to the data. The report supplies risks in exposed and unexposed groups, and the team is reviewing the comparison.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: What risk ratio compares exposed with unexposed participants for the clinical outcome in the constructed cohort?

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: Divide exposed risk by unexposed risk: 0.20/0.10 = 2.0. The inputs are probabilities, so the result is a risk ratio.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 2.0
answerChoices.rationale: The quotient 0.20/0.10 compares risks, not odds. Calling that number an odds ratio changes the scale without doing an odds calculation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The quotient 0.20/0.10 compares risks, not odds. Calling that number an odds ratio changes the scale without doing an odds calculation.

answerChoices.label: Risk ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: The value 0.5 comes from 0.10/0.20, reversing the requested exposed-versus-unexposed direction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The value 0.5 comes from 0.10/0.20, reversing the requested exposed-versus-unexposed direction.

answerChoices.label: Odds ratio of 0.5
answerChoices.rationale: This both reverses the comparison and assigns an odds label to a calculation of probabilities. Neither change preserves the requested estimate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This both reverses the comparison and assigns an odds label to a calculation of probabilities. Neither change preserves the requested estimate.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: Dividing the exposed risk by the unexposed risk gives 0.20/0.10 = 2.0, a risk ratio. That calculation does not become an odds ratio by relabeling it.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: Risk is a probability; a risk ratio divides one group's probability by the comparator's. Here 20%/10% = 2.0 for exposed versus unexposed over 30 days. An odds ratio compares odds instead. Remember both the scale and direction: reversing the groups gives a reciprocal, while changing the label changes the claimed measure.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: Which association measure can be calculated directly from the case-control exposure table for postoperative leak?

answerChoices.label: Exposure odds ratio of 1.8
answerChoices.rationale: Compare exposure odds in cases and controls: (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8. This gives an exposure odds ratio for the supplied outcome-selected sample.

answerChoices.label: Exposure risk ratio of 1.8
answerChoices.rationale: The sampling plan selects cases and controls by outcome. Their totals do not provide the population risks needed to justify a risk-ratio label.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The sampling plan selects cases and controls by outcome. Their totals do not provide the population risks needed to justify a risk-ratio label.

answerChoices.label: Exposure odds ratio of 0.56
answerChoices.rationale: About 0.56 is the reciprocal of 1.8. It describes controls versus cases, reversing the requested exposure-odds comparison.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: About 0.56 is the reciprocal of 1.8. It describes controls versus cases, reversing the requested exposure-odds comparison.

answerChoices.label: Exposure risk ratio of 0.56
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the direction and uses a risk scale unsupported by the outcome-selected sampling totals.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the direction and uses a risk scale unsupported by the outcome-selected sampling totals.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: The exposure odds ratio is (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8 for cases versus controls. Population risks are not supplied, so a risk-ratio label is unsupported.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: In this outcome-selected table, compare exposure odds in cases with exposure odds in controls: (18/12)/(10/12) = 1.8. That is an exposure odds ratio. The sampled case and control totals do not supply population event risks. Remember what the design selected before deciding whether a risk-ratio label is justified.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the skin-oncology discussion lead, reviews a new biologic for Merkel cell carcinoma. An adjusted model reports recurrence odds over two years. The representative offers to simplify the statistics by removing the parts customers ask about. question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: How should the adjusted odds ratio of 0.60 for two-year recurrence be described when group risks are unavailable?

answerChoices.label: Adjusted odds are 0.60 times as high
answerChoices.rationale: The reported adjusted odds ratio is 0.60. Describing the adjusted odds as 0.60 times the comparison odds keeps the estimate on its reported scale.

answerChoices.label: Adjusted risk is exactly 0.60 times as high
answerChoices.rationale: The model reports odds, not an exact ratio of probabilities. Group risks needed for that asserted risk comparison are not supplied.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The model reports odds, not an exact ratio of probabilities. Group risks needed for that asserted risk comparison are not supplied.

answerChoices.label: Absolute risk falls by 40 percentage points
answerChoices.rationale: An odds ratio alone does not provide an absolute risk difference. Subtracting it from one cannot create a 40-percentage-point reduction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An odds ratio alone does not provide an absolute risk difference. Subtracting it from one cannot create a 40-percentage-point reduction.

answerChoices.label: Adjusted event probability is 40% lower
answerChoices.rationale: An odds ratio of 0.60 cannot automatically be translated into a 40% reduction in event probability. That changes odds into risk without the needed information.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An odds ratio of 0.60 cannot automatically be translated into a 40% reduction in event probability. That changes odds into risk without the needed information.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: The estimate describes adjusted odds at 0.60 times the comparison odds. Without group risks, it cannot provide the asserted exact risk ratio or absolute risk reduction.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: Odds and probability are different scales. An adjusted odds ratio of 0.60 says the compared odds are 0.60 times the reference odds, within the reported model. It does not supply the same proportional probability reduction or an absolute risk difference. Keep the measure's name attached to its number when translating a report.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the bariatric journal-club lead, reviews a new protective agent for marginal ulcer after gastric bypass. The observational report labels its estimate as an exposure odds ratio for rare ulcer recurrence. The editor requests a more exciting conclusion while retaining 'strictly factual.' Underlying group risks are unavailable, and the investigators discuss approximate similarity to a risk ratio.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.stem: Which interpretation preserves the reported measure when an exposure odds ratio for rare ulcer recurrence is discussed as approximately similar to a risk ratio?

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as an odds ratio
answerChoices.rationale: The report actually estimates an odds ratio. Retaining its label preserves the measure despite the stated approximate similarity for this rare outcome.

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as a relative risk
answerChoices.rationale: Approximate similarity does not establish an exact risk ratio. Baseline risks for a direct risk comparison are not supplied.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Approximate similarity does not establish an exact risk ratio. Baseline risks for a direct risk comparison are not supplied.

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as a relative risk reduction
answerChoices.rationale: A relative risk reduction is a different claim from the reported odds ratio. The supplied information does not justify relabeling the measure that way.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A relative risk reduction is a different claim from the reported odds ratio. The supplied information does not justify relabeling the measure that way.

answerChoices.label: Report the estimate as an absolute risk difference
answerChoices.rationale: An absolute risk difference requires probabilities to subtract. The reported odds ratio and missing baseline risks do not supply those values.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An absolute risk difference requires probabilities to subtract. The reported odds ratio and missing baseline risks do not supply those values.

question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.explanation: Report the estimate as an odds ratio. The stated approximate similarity does not convert it into an exact risk ratio or supply an absolute risk difference.
question.statistics-ethics.risk-ratio-od.teachingPoint: Approximate similarity is not permission to rename an estimate. The report gives an odds ratio, so retain that label even when discussing a rare outcome. Without the underlying risks, the exhibit does not supply an exact risk ratio or an absolute difference. A useful reporting rule is to preserve the scale you actually estimated.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v1.stem: For colon-cancer recurrence over two years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Subtracting gives 0.10; 1/0.10 = 10 for the specified outcome over two years.

answerChoices.label: ARR 50 percentage points; NNT 2 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The outcome risk halves relative to its 20% starting value, but falls by 10 percentage points, not 50. The relative wording does not supply this ARR or NNT.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The outcome risk halves relative to its 20% starting value, but falls by 10 percentage points, not 50. The relative wording does not supply this ARR or NNT.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 100 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: The absolute difference is right, but its reciprocal uses the proportion 0.10: 1/0.10 = 10, not 100.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The absolute difference is right, but its reciprocal uses the proportion 0.10: 1/0.10 = 10, not 100.

answerChoices.label: ARR 5 percentage points; NNT 20 over two years
answerChoices.rationale: An NNT of 20 would correspond to an absolute difference of 0.05. These practice risks differ by 0.10 instead.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An NNT of 20 would correspond to an absolute difference of 0.05. These practice risks differ by 0.10 instead.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v1.explanation: The practice risks are 20/100 and 10/100. Their difference is 0.10, giving ARR 10 percentage points and NNT 10 for the specified two-year outcome.
question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v1.teachingPoint: Calculate each group's risk first, then subtract intervention risk from comparator risk. Here 20% minus 10% is 10 percentage points, so NNT is 1/0.10 = 10 over two years. Half the starting risk and a 10-point absolute drop describe the same practice numbers; keep the outcome, comparator, and period attached.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v2.stem: For cutaneous-SCC recurrence over three years in the constructed trial, what ARR and NNT describe the new unnamed intervention versus control?

answerChoices.label: ARR 33 percentage points; NNT 3 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: About 33% describes the relative reduction from 15% to 10%. The absolute drop is five percentage points, giving NNT 20.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: About 33% describes the relative reduction from 15% to 10%. The absolute drop is five percentage points, giving NNT 20.

answerChoices.label: ARR 10 percentage points; NNT 10 over three years
answerChoices.rationale: The comparator risk is 30/200 = 15%, not 20%. Using the actual denominator gives a five-point difference rather than ten.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The comparator risk is 30/200 = 15%, not 20%. Using the actual denominator gives a five-point difference rather than ten.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v2.explanation: First calculate risks: 30/200 = 0.15 and 10/100 = 0.10. ARR is 0.05, or five percentage points, and three-year NNT is 20.
question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v2.teachingPoint: Unequal group sizes make raw event-count subtraction misleading. Convert each count to a risk: 30/200 = 15% and 10/100 = 10%. Their absolute difference is five percentage points, so NNT is 1/0.05 = 20 over three years. Remember: divide within groups before subtracting between groups, retaining the specified recurrence outcome and comparator.

question.statistics-ethics.arr-nnt.v4.teachingPoint: Subtract the risks before taking a reciprocal: 20% minus 14% is six percentage points, or 0.06. Then 1/0.06 is about 16.67; conventionally round NNT upward to 17. Keep the specified recurrence outcome, comparator, and two-year period with the result. The intervention's 14% risk is not itself the reduction.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v1.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the biliary journal-club lead, reviews a new dissection instrument used in acute cholecystitis operations. The trial compares thirty-day surgical-site infection and reports its preplanned analysis. Investigators specified the null model before collecting outcomes. question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v1.stem: Which interpretation is justified by the reported p-value for thirty-day SSI in the constructed trial?

answerChoices.label: A 3% chance of results this extreme or more under the null model
answerChoices.rationale: Assume the specified null model and analysis conditions. Results this incompatible with that model, or more so, have probability 0.03; the probability is conditional on the model.

answerChoices.label: A 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses the conditioning. The p-value assumes the null model to evaluate data, rather than assigning a 3% probability to the null hypothesis after observing data.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses the conditioning. The p-value assumes the null model to evaluate data, rather than assigning a 3% probability to the null hypothesis after observing data.

answerChoices.label: A 97% probability that the intervention truly changed the outcome after observing these results
answerChoices.rationale: One minus p does not supply a posterior probability that the intervention truly changed scores. The complement 0.97 is not that truth probability.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: One minus p does not supply a posterior probability that the intervention truly changed scores. The complement 0.97 is not that truth probability.

answerChoices.label: An estimated difference of 0.03 outcome units between the two groups being compared
answerChoices.rationale: The 0.03 is a probability under a null model, not a difference in outcome units. Read the effect magnitude from its separately reported estimate.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The 0.03 is a probability under a null model, not a difference in outcome units. Read the effect magnitude from its separately reported estimate.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v1.explanation: Under the specified null model, results this extreme or more have probability 0.03. That is neither the probability of a true null nor the size of the clinical difference.
question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v1.teachingPoint: A null model is the comparison's starting assumption. A p-value asks how probable data this incompatible with that model, or more so, would be under the model and analysis conditions. Here that probability is 0.03. Remember: probability of data under a model is not probability that the model is true, and is not effect size.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: A probability under the null model is not a 0.40-unit outcome difference. Effect magnitude requires its own estimate.

A p-value describes the probability of data this extreme or more if that model and its analysis assumptions hold. Here that probability is 0.40. Neither p nor one minus p gives the probability of no effect. Effect size requires a separate estimate.

answerChoices.label: The result does not prove exact equality
answerChoices.rationale: The p-value does not prove a zero group difference. The exact-equality sentence claims more than the reported probability establishes.

answerChoices.label: The result favors equal group effects

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Failure to establish a difference is not proof or a supplied probability of equality. The p-value alone does not settle whether the means are exactly equal.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: The 0.08 describes data conditional on a null model, not an 8% probability that no effect exists after observing the data.

question.statistics-ethics.p-value.v4.explanation: The reported p-value does not prove exact equality. It also does not give an 8% probability of no effect or establish that any difference is clinically small.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the groin-surgery research lead, reviews a new reinforcement material for femoral hernia repair. The trial reports recurrence within two years as a risk ratio with an interval. The sponsor welcomes uncertainty in principle, but asks whether it can be moved to the appendix. The team is reviewing how the reported range relates to the no-difference value.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.stem: How does the constructed two-year recurrence risk-ratio interval relate to its null value, and what interpretation is justified?

answerChoices.label: The interval includes the null value 1
answerChoices.rationale: One lies between 0.40 and 1.20, so the interval includes the no-association value for a ratio. Inclusion does not establish an exactly true ratio of one.

answerChoices.label: The interval excludes the null value 1
answerChoices.rationale: The upper limit is 1.20 and the lower limit is 0.40. One is inside these limits, so it is not excluded.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The upper limit is 1.20 and the lower limit is 0.40. One is inside these limits, so it is not excluded.

answerChoices.label: The interval gives 95% probability of a real association
answerChoices.rationale: The 95% level describes coverage of the interval method. It does not give a 95% probability that an association is real.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The 95% level describes coverage of the interval method. It does not give a 95% probability that an association is real.

answerChoices.label: The interval supports an exactly absent association
answerChoices.rationale: An interval containing one is compatible with the ratio null value, but also contains other ratios. It does not prove that the association is exactly absent.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: An interval containing one is compatible with the ratio null value, but also contains other ratios. It does not prove that the association is exactly absent.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.explanation: The ratio interval from 0.40 to 1.20 contains 1. It is compatible with the ratio null value, without proving an exactly absent association.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.teachingPoint: For a ratio, the no-association value is 1, because the compared quantities are equal. One falls within 0.40 to 1.20, so this interval includes that null value. Inclusion is not proof that the true ratio is exactly 1. Remember the measure's scale before looking for its null value.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the colorectal journal-club lead, reviews a new operative closure technique for chronic pilonidal disease. question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.stem: Which statement is justified by the constructed two-year recurrence risk difference of -4 percentage points with a 95% interval from -6 to -2?

answerChoices.label: The interval excludes the null value 0
answerChoices.rationale: All values from -6 to -2 are below zero. The interval therefore excludes zero, the no-difference value on this scale.

answerChoices.label: The interval includes the null value 0
answerChoices.rationale: Zero is outside the stated limits. The null for a difference is zero, even though a ratio would use one.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Zero is outside the stated limits. The null for a difference is zero, even though a ratio would use one.

answerChoices.label: The interval gives 95% probability of clinical benefit
answerChoices.rationale: The confidence level is not a probability that the intervention provides clinical benefit. The exercise gives no clinical-importance criterion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The confidence level is not a probability that the intervention provides clinical benefit. The exercise gives no clinical-importance criterion.

answerChoices.label: The interval establishes a clinically important effect
answerChoices.rationale: Excluding zero addresses compatibility with the difference null. It does not, by itself, establish a clinically important magnitude.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Excluding zero addresses compatibility with the difference null. It does not, by itself, establish a clinically important magnitude.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.explanation: The interval from -6 to -2 excludes zero, the null for a risk difference. Excluding zero does not by itself establish a clinically important effect.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.teachingPoint: For a difference, the no-difference value is 0, rather than the ratio null of 1. Every value from -6 to -2 lies below zero, so this interval excludes the null. That describes the estimate's uncertainty on its stated scale; it does not alone establish clinical importance or a probability of benefit.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the breast-service research lead, reviews two studies of a new aspiration device for lactational breast abscesses. Both report repeat drainage within thirty days on the same scale. A colleague prefers the paper with the most confident title; its author underlined 'definitive' twice. The intervals use the same method and confidence level, and the team is comparing precision.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.stem: Which constructed repeat-drainage risk-difference interval is more precise when method, confidence level and measurement scale are the same?

answerChoices.label: The 4-to-6 interval is more precise
answerChoices.rationale: The 4-to-6 interval is narrower than 1-to-9 under the same method, confidence level, and scale. It therefore displays greater sampling precision.

answerChoices.label: The 1-to-9 interval is more precise
answerChoices.rationale: The 1-to-9 interval is wider. Under the supplied comparable conditions, that width displays more sampling uncertainty rather than greater precision.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The 1-to-9 interval is wider. Under the supplied comparable conditions, that width displays more sampling uncertainty rather than greater precision.

answerChoices.label: Both intervals have equal precision
answerChoices.rationale: Both point estimates are five, but the interval widths differ. A shared center does not imply equal precision.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Both point estimates are five, but the interval widths differ. A shared center does not imply equal precision.

answerChoices.label: Precision cannot be ranked without sample sizes
answerChoices.rationale: The widths already display relative sampling precision under the same method and scale. The exercise does not require sample sizes to compare those widths.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The widths already display relative sampling precision under the same method and scale. The exercise does not require sample sizes to compare those widths.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.explanation: The 4-to-6 interval is more precise because it is narrower under the same method and scale. Both estimates being 5 does not equalize the interval widths.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.teachingPoint: With the same method, confidence level, and scale, a narrower interval displays less sampling uncertainty and therefore greater precision. The 4-to-6 interval is narrower than 1-to-9, even though both center on 5. Remember that the center gives the point estimate while the width conveys precision; equal centers do not imply equal uncertainty.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the upper-GI journal-club lead, reviews a new biologic after resection of gastric adenocarcinoma. Its trial reports a three-year recurrence risk difference with a frequentist interval. The presenter lists an invited lecture on his CV; the invitation came from the seminar series he organizes himself. The team is reviewing what the stated confidence level describes across repeated studies.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.stem: What does a 95% confidence level describe for repeated use of the stated frequentist three-year recurrence risk-difference interval procedure?

answerChoices.label: The method covers the true value in 95% of repetitions
answerChoices.rationale: The 95% level describes long-run coverage by intervals constructed with this procedure under its assumptions. The fixed true value is covered in that proportion of repetitions.

answerChoices.label: This interval has a 95% chance of containing the truth
answerChoices.rationale: After observation, this frequentist framework treats the parameter as fixed. Its confidence level does not assign a fresh probability to this particular interval containing that value.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: After observation, this frequentist framework treats the parameter as fixed. Its confidence level does not assign a fresh probability to this particular interval containing that value.

answerChoices.label: The null hypothesis has a 5% chance of being correct
answerChoices.rationale: Neither 95% confidence nor its 5% complement supplies a truth probability for a hypothesis. That is a different question from interval coverage.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Neither 95% confidence nor its 5% complement supplies a truth probability for a hypothesis. That is a different question from interval coverage.

answerChoices.label: The estimate has a 95% chance of being unbiased
answerChoices.rationale: Coverage under a procedure does not guarantee the absence of systematic bias. The confidence level is not a probability that the estimate is unbiased.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Coverage under a procedure does not guarantee the absence of systematic bias. The confidence level is not a probability that the estimate is unbiased.

question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.explanation: The 95% refers to long-run coverage of intervals produced by the procedure under its assumptions. It does not assign a 95% truth probability to this particular interval.
question.statistics-ethics.confidence-in.teachingPoint: A frequentist confidence level describes repeated use of the interval method under its assumptions. In 95% of those repetitions, intervals produced by the procedure cover the fixed true value. It is a property of the method, not a new probability assigned to this observed interval or a guarantee that the estimate is unbiased.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..patientPresentation: {patientName}, the breast-oncology research lead, reviews a new local treatment device for DCIS. A simulation concerns recurrence within five years and stipulates the underlying state. The investigator lists one conference abstract as a presentation, publication and public-engagement project on his appraisal. The analysis rejects its null, and the team is reviewing how to classify that simulated result.
question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..stem: Which testing error occurs in the simulated DCIS-recurrence analysis when the null is true but the analysis rejects it?

answerChoices.label: Type I error
answerChoices.rationale: The underlying null is stipulated to be true, yet the analysis rejects it. That truth-and-decision combination defines a type I error.

answerChoices.label: Type II error
answerChoices.rationale: Type II error would mean failing to reject under a specified true alternative. Both the underlying state and decision differ from this exhibit.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Type II error would mean failing to reject under a specified true alternative. Both the underlying state and decision differ from this exhibit.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit gives the hypothesis state and decision, without describing inconsistent outcome measurement. It identifies a testing error rather than that bias mechanism.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit gives the hypothesis state and decision, without describing inconsistent outcome measurement. It identifies a testing error rather than that bias mechanism.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias
answerChoices.rationale: No systematic exclusion from recruitment is supplied. The stated problem is rejection of a true null, not a selection process.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No systematic exclusion from recruitment is supplied. The stated problem is rejection of a true null, not a selection process.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..explanation: Rejecting a true null is a type I error. The exhibit supplies the true state and testing decision, not evidence of a measurement or recruitment mechanism.
question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..teachingPoint: Testing errors compare a decision with the underlying state. Type I error means rejecting a null that is actually true; type II means failing to reject when a specified alternative is true. Here the null is true and was rejected. Remember: first identify what is true, then what the analysis decided.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..patientPresentation: {patientName}, the liver-surgery discussion lead, reviews a new resection instrument for solitary hepatocellular carcinoma in a favorable operative profile. A simulation concerns recurrence within three years and stipulates that a specified difference exists. The analysis fails to reject its null model. question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..stem: Which testing error occurs in the simulated HCC-recurrence analysis when the specified alternative is true but the analysis fails to reject the null?

answerChoices.label: Type II error
answerChoices.rationale: The specified alternative is stipulated to be true, but the test fails to reject the null. That combination defines a type II error.

answerChoices.label: Type I error
answerChoices.rationale: Type I error requires rejection under a true null. This exercise instead supplies nonrejection under a true alternative.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Type I error requires rejection under a true null. This exercise instead supplies nonrejection under a true alternative.

answerChoices.label: Measurement bias
answerChoices.rationale: No unequal outcome-recording process is described. The facts identify a missed specified alternative by the test.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No unequal outcome-recording process is described. The facts identify a missed specified alternative by the test.

answerChoices.label: Selection bias
answerChoices.rationale: The exhibit does not describe systematic sampling exclusion. The testing decision, compared with the supplied true alternative, identifies the error.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The exhibit does not describe systematic sampling exclusion. The testing decision, compared with the supplied true alternative, identifies the error.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..explanation: This is a type II error: the specified alternative is true, yet the test fails to reject the null. Nonrejection does not establish that no effect exists.
question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..teachingPoint: Failure to reject does not guarantee a true null. If the specified alternative is actually true and the analysis misses it, the decision is a type II error. Type I is the opposite truth-and-decision combination: rejection under a true null. Keep the underlying state separate from the decision reported by the test.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..patientPresentation: {patientName}, the pancreatic-oncology research lead, reviews a new radiation-delivery technique after pancreatic tail cancer resection. Its trial is planned around recurrence within two years. The grant writer wants a guaranteed discovery and asks whether 'statistically likely' can be upgraded in the budget justification. The calculation specifies the effect, variability and sampling assumptions before any outcomes are collected.
question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..stem: What does prospective power describe under the specified alternative in the constructed pancreatic-cancer recurrence trial?

answerChoices.label: Chance of rejection if that alternative is true
answerChoices.rationale: Under the specified true alternative and design assumptions, power is the probability of rejecting the null. It describes how the planned procedure behaves in that situation.

answerChoices.label: Chance that a statistically positive result is true
answerChoices.rationale: This reverses what is conditioned on. Power assumes an alternative to evaluate rejection, rather than estimating whether a statistically positive conclusion is true.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This reverses what is conditioned on. Power assumes an alternative to evaluate rejection, rather than estimating whether a statistically positive conclusion is true.

answerChoices.label: Chance that the null hypothesis itself is true
answerChoices.rationale: The plan does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis being true. It calculates a rejection probability under the specified alternative.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The plan does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis being true. It calculates a rejection probability under the specified alternative.

answerChoices.label: Chance of nonrejection if that alternative is true
answerChoices.rationale: Nonrejection under a true alternative describes a type II error probability. Power instead concerns rejection under that alternative.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Nonrejection under a true alternative describes a type II error probability. Power instead concerns rejection under that alternative.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..explanation: Planned power is the chance of rejecting the null under the specified true alternative and design assumptions. It is not the truth probability of a positive result.
question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..teachingPoint: Power is the probability that the analysis rejects the null if the specified alternative is true, under the planned design assumptions. It is a statement about a procedure operating in that situation. Remember the direction of conditioning: it does not give the probability that a positive study conclusion or the alternative itself is true.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..patientPresentation: {patientName}, the skin-oncology journal-club lead, reviews a new topical agent for basal cell carcinoma. The trial evaluates recurrence within two years and does not reject its null model. After seeing the results, authors calculate low power and conclude the agent has no effect. question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..stem: Which statement is justified when the constructed basal-cell-carcinoma recurrence trial fails to reject its null and reports low post-hoc power?

answerChoices.label: Post-hoc power does not prove no effect
answerChoices.rationale: A low post-hoc calculation does not establish that the effect is exactly absent. Power is conditional on a specified alternative, rather than a truth probability for the null.

answerChoices.label: Low post-hoc power favors an absent effect
answerChoices.rationale: The later calculation does not make the no-effect conclusion valid. Neither low post-hoc power nor nonrejection supplies proof of an absent effect.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The later calculation does not make the no-effect conclusion valid. Neither low post-hoc power nor nonrejection supplies proof of an absent effect.

answerChoices.label: Post-hoc power gives the probability of the null
answerChoices.rationale: Power does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis. It concerns rejection behavior under a specified alternative.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Power does not assign a probability to the null hypothesis. It concerns rejection behavior under a specified alternative.

answerChoices.label: The observed p-value is the study's achieved power
answerChoices.rationale: A p-value concerns observed-or-more-extreme data under a null model; power concerns rejection under an alternative. They are different conditional quantities.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A p-value concerns observed-or-more-extreme data under a null model; power concerns rejection under an alternative. They are different conditional quantities.

question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..explanation: Low post-hoc power does not prove no effect. It neither gives the probability of the null nor makes the observed p-value equal to power.
question.statistics-ethics.errors-power..teachingPoint: Power describes rejection probability under a specified alternative, not the probability that a hypothesis is true. A low post-hoc power calculation after nonrejection does not establish an exactly absent effect. Remember that a second conditional calculation cannot transform the first result into proof of equality or supply the effect size missing from this exercise.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the GI improvement lead, reviews an authorized pilot of a new dietitian care pathway for celiac disease. The results describe only the tested local setting.
question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.stem: Which Act-step decision fits the authorized celiac pathway pilot when its symptom aim is met and the balancing measure does not worsen?

answerChoices.label: Adopt locally and plan the next test
answerChoices.rationale: The test met its aim without worsening balance in the tested setting. Local adoption uses that learning while a next linked test investigates the next step.

answerChoices.label: Spread the change and monitor other clinics
answerChoices.rationale: The results apply to the local test. Spreading immediately to other clinics goes beyond that scope instead of testing the next setting.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The results apply to the local test. Spreading immediately to other clinics goes beyond that scope instead of testing the next setting.

answerChoices.label: Repeat the same pilot before making any change
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied favorable aim and balancing findings support local action. Repeating the identical pilot without acting does not use the stated learning.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The supplied favorable aim and balancing findings support local action. Repeating the identical pilot without acting does not use the stated learning.

answerChoices.label: Adapt the pathway before another local test
answerChoices.rationale: The findings identify no feature requiring revision before local adoption. Adaptation needs a reason in the learning, rather than a change for its own sake.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The findings identify no feature requiring revision before local adoption. Adaptation needs a reason in the learning, rather than a change for its own sake.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.explanation: Adopt the successful pathway locally and plan the next linked test. The favorable aim and balancing findings apply to the tested setting, not an untested wider rollout.
question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.teachingPoint: The Act step turns learning into a decision and a next test. This pathway version met its aim without worsening the balancing measure, supporting local adoption and a linked next cycle. Keep the scope of action tied to the scope of the evidence: a successful small test does not automatically establish performance at every clinic.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.patientPresentation: {patientName}, the wound-service improvement lead, reviews an authorized new compression-device pilot for venous leg ulcers after adequate arterial assessment. question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.stem: Which Act-step decision fits the authorized venous-ulcer device pilot when healing is faster but application rework doubles?

answerChoices.label: Adapt device use and retest locally
answerChoices.rationale: Healing improved but rework doubled. Revise device use to address that burden and use the next test to study the adapted version.

answerChoices.label: Adopt device use and monitor application rework
answerChoices.rationale: Adopting this version unchanged accepts the documented worsening of rework. The balancing finding calls for adaptation before adoption.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Adopting this version unchanged accepts the documented worsening of rework. The balancing finding calls for adaptation before adoption.

answerChoices.label: Abandon device use and test another local idea
answerChoices.rationale: The target improvement supports retaining and adapting the idea. The supplied findings do not require discarding it instead of addressing the added burden.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The target improvement supports retaining and adapting the idea. The supplied findings do not require discarding it instead of addressing the added burden.

answerChoices.label: Repeat device use without revising the process
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the same device unchanged does not respond to the increased rework already observed. The next cycle should use that learning.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating the same device unchanged does not respond to the increased rework already observed. The next cycle should use that learning.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.teachingPoint: Improvement needs both the intended result and a check for shifted burden. This device shortened wound-closure time but doubled rework, so adapt its use and retest rather than adopting the current version unchanged. The Act step can preserve a promising idea while changing the part that caused trouble. Learning should change the next cycle.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.stem: Which Act-step decision fits the authorized gastroparesis pathway pilot when its symptom aim is not met and care planning takes longer, with no specific correctable defect identified?

answerChoices.label: Abandon this version and test another idea

answerChoices.label: Adapt the pathway labels and repeat this version

answerChoices.distractorRationale: The observations do not identify a labeling problem to fix. That specific adaptation invents an explanation rather than using the supplied findings.

answerChoices.label: Adopt the pathway and monitor the next cycle

answerChoices.distractorRationale: The tested version missed the aim and increased care-planning time, so the evidence does not support adopting it while monitoring later.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.stem: Which Act-step decision fits the authorized wrist-bracing pathway pilot when missing hand-function observations prevent judging its stated aim?

answerChoices.label: Fix data capture and repeat a bounded test
answerChoices.rationale: The missing observations prevent judging the aim. Repair data capture and repeat a bounded test so the next decision rests on interpretable results.

answerChoices.label: Adopt the change and improve later measurement
answerChoices.rationale: The incomplete records do not establish success. Adopting first and measuring later turns an information gap into an unsupported favorable verdict.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The incomplete records do not establish success. Adopting first and measuring later turns an information gap into an unsupported favorable verdict.

answerChoices.label: Adapt the intervention before collecting more data
answerChoices.rationale: The data gap does not identify an intervention feature to adapt. Fixing measurement addresses the known problem before choosing a specific revision.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The data gap does not identify an intervention feature to adapt. Fixing measurement addresses the known problem before choosing a specific revision.

answerChoices.label: Abandon the change and test a different idea
answerChoices.rationale: Incomplete measurement does not establish that the intervention failed. Abandonment would turn missing evidence into an unsupported unfavorable verdict.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Incomplete measurement does not establish that the intervention failed. Abandonment would turn missing evidence into an unsupported unfavorable verdict.

question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.explanation: Fix data capture and repeat a bounded test. The missing observations prevent judging this intervention; they do not establish either success or failure.
question.quality-improvement.pdsa-act-an.teachingPoint: An uninterpretable test needs better measurement before an intervention verdict. Here missing observations prevent judging the aim, so repair data capture and repeat a bounded test. Remember the distinction between evidence of failure and failure to collect evidence; the latter does not establish adoption, adaptation, or abandonment of the intervention itself.

question.statistics-ethics.qi-measures.v.stem: Which set lists a process measure, the intended clinical outcome measure and a balancing measure, in that order, for the ileostomy rehydration device pilot?

answerChoices.label: Device use as planned; dehydration episodes; application workload
answerChoices.rationale: Device use tracks implementation, dehydration episodes track the clinical aim, and application workload checks an unwanted tradeoff in delivering the intervention.

answerChoices.label: Dehydration episodes; device use as planned; application workload
answerChoices.rationale: Dehydration episodes measure the clinical outcome, while device use measures implementation. This ordering reverses process and outcome.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Dehydration episodes measure the clinical outcome, while device use measures implementation. This ordering reverses process and outcome.

answerChoices.label: Device use as planned; application workload; dehydration episodes
answerChoices.rationale: Application workload checks a tradeoff, while dehydration episodes is the aim; this ordering swaps outcome and balancing measures.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Application workload checks a tradeoff, while dehydration episodes is the aim; this ordering swaps outcome and balancing measures.

answerChoices.label: Application workload; dehydration episodes; device use as planned
answerChoices.rationale: Application workload belongs in the balancing position, while device use as planned belongs first; this ordering places both incorrectly.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Application workload belongs in the balancing position, while device use as planned belongs first; this ordering places both incorrectly.

question.statistics-ethics.qi-measures.v.explanation: Device use tracks implementation, dehydration episodes track the clinical aim, and application workload checks a tradeoff. Counting applications alone does not establish a clinical improvement.
question.statistics-ethics.qi-measures.v.teachingPoint: A process measure asks whether planned care happened; an outcome measure asks whether patients experienced the intended result. A balancing measure checks an unwanted tradeoff. Here device use, dehydration and workload answer those three questions. Remember: delivery, result, tradeoff. More device applications alone would not establish that dehydration improved.

answerChoices.label: Completed program screening; extra diagnostic visits; missed cancers at follow-up
answerChoices.rationale: Extra diagnostic visits check burden, while missed cancers measure the aim. This ordering swaps the outcome and balancing positions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Extra diagnostic visits check burden, while missed cancers measure the aim. This ordering swaps the outcome and balancing positions.

answerChoices.label: Missed cancers at follow-up; completed program screening; extra diagnostic visits
answerChoices.rationale: Missed cancers are the outcome and completed screening is process. This set places those two measures in the reverse order requested.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Missed cancers are the outcome and completed screening is process. This set places those two measures in the reverse order requested.

question.statistics-ethics.qi-measures.v.explanation: Use completed program screening as process, missed cancers at follow-up as outcome, and extra diagnostic visits as balance. Attendance counts do not substitute for the diagnostic aim.
question.statistics-ethics.qi-measures.v.teachingPoint: Screening activity and screening success need different measures. Completed screens track delivery; missed cancers at follow-up track the stated diagnostic aim; extra diagnostic visits check burden. Remember to count both what the program does and what it misses. Invitation or attendance totals alone do not establish that the clinical aim improved.

question.statistics-ethics.qualified-int.stem: Before discussing laparoscopic cholecystectomy for {patientName}'s symptomatic gallstones, what communication support is needed when patient and surgeon cannot communicate adequately?

answerChoices.label: Arrange qualified Spanish interpretation
answerChoices.rationale: Qualified Spanish interpretation supports an understandable discussion and the patient's own questions. Neither the child's offer nor the employee's bilingual skill establishes competence to interpret clinical information.

answerChoices.label: Use the child's interpretation for consent
answerChoices.rationale: The child wants to help, but willingness does not establish the competence needed for this clinical consent discussion. The patient still needs qualified interpretation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The child wants to help, but willingness does not establish the competence needed for this clinical consent discussion. The patient still needs qualified interpretation.

answerChoices.label: Ask a bilingual clinic clerk to interpret
answerChoices.rationale: Speaking Spanish is not itself evidence of competence to interpret clinical information. The employee's qualification has not been established.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Speaking Spanish is not itself evidence of competence to interpret clinical information. The employee's qualification has not been established.

answerChoices.label: Use a translated Spanish consent handout
answerChoices.rationale: Written information can support the discussion, but cannot provide the qualified two-way exchange needed for the patient's own clinical questions.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Written information can support the discussion, but cannot provide the qualified two-way exchange needed for the patient's own clinical questions.

question.statistics-ethics.qualified-int.explanation: Arrange qualified Spanish interpretation so the patient can discuss the proposed cholecystectomy and ask questions. Neither the child's willingness nor the employee's bilingual conversation establishes interpreter competence.
question.statistics-ethics.qualified-int.teachingPoint: Consent needs an understandable conversation, including the patient's own questions. When patient and clinician cannot communicate adequately, arrange qualified interpretation. A child's offer or an employee's conversational bilingual skill does not establish that competence. Make the conversation possible before asking for a decision; written materials can support, but cannot replace, that exchange.

question.statistics-ethics.informed-cons.reachedCurrentUpdate: With qualified Spanish interpretation, {patientName}, a {patientAge}-year-old {patientSex}, has recurrent symptoms with ultrasound-confirmed gallstones and is discussing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. A signed form lists the operation, but material risks, benefits and alternatives have not been discussed. The surgeon calls the form self-explanatory, then asks the nurse to explain its instructions. The patient has questions before agreeing to surgery.
question.statistics-ethics.informed-cons.stem: With qualified interpretation in place, what is needed for informed consent to {patientName}'s laparoscopic cholecystectomy when material information has not been discussed?

answerChoices.label: Discuss risks, benefits, and alternatives
answerChoices.rationale: The patient lacks the clinical information needed to choose. Discuss the intervention's relevant risks, benefits, and alternatives, including foregoing it, in an understandable conversation.

answerChoices.label: Confirm the form was signed voluntarily
answerChoices.rationale: Voluntary signing matters, but confirming it does not supply the omitted risks, benefits, and alternatives. Information and voluntariness are separate needs.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Voluntary signing matters, but confirming it does not supply the omitted risks, benefits, and alternatives. Information and voluntariness are separate needs.

answerChoices.label: Have the patient reread the consent document
answerChoices.rationale: Rereading the document does not by itself supply the clinical conversation that never occurred. A form can document consent without replacing the discussion.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Rereading the document does not by itself supply the clinical conversation that never occurred. A form can document consent without replacing the discussion.

answerChoices.label: Ask the patient to describe the planned operation
answerChoices.rationale: Describing the procedure's purpose checks only part of understanding. The stated gaps about relevant risks, benefits, and alternatives remain.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Describing the procedure's purpose checks only part of understanding. The stated gaps about relevant risks, benefits, and alternatives remain.

question.statistics-ethics.informed-cons.explanation: The missing step is an understandable discussion of the intervention, risks, benefits, and alternatives. Confirming a signature or willingness alone does not fill those information gaps.
question.statistics-ethics.informed-cons.teachingPoint: Informed consent helps a person understand the intervention, its relevant risks and benefits, and alternatives including declining, so the person can choose voluntarily. A signature cannot replace that conversation. The patient needs that discussion before the form can be relied on for the operation. Remember: document the conversation, rather than substituting a document for it.
